roots.name: Breadbin case: two-piece ABS shell
roots.description: The C64 'breadbin' housing is a rear shell and a front bezel, both injection-moulded general-purpose ABS in a warm beige-brown. The rear shell carries the ventilation ribs, moulded screw bosses, connector cut-outs and the rubber feet; the bezel carries the keyboard window with its square key openings, the two knurled thumbscrews, the rainbow badge and the fine 'leather' grain. A foil-on-board RFI shield sits inside over the motherboard.
roots.note: The case is universally reported as ABS - it is the polymer that browns under UV and can be reversed with peroxide 'retrobright' bleaching. Commodore's own 2025 C64 Ultimate copy notes the surviving tooling carries a 'period-correct 2-point flow pattern'.

children.name: Rear shell (bottom half)
children.description: The larger of the two mouldings. It forms the base pan, the raised side walls, the wrap-over top with its row of ventilation slots, the rear and side connector cut-outs, the internal ribs that stiffen the pan, the moulded screw bosses and standoffs, and the feet pads.

facts.label: Parting line
facts.value: along the top flange, visible as a faint seam

children.name: Ventilation slots in the top wrap
children.description: A row of moulded louvre slots in the curved top panel behind the cartridge port, letting convective air out of the case over the SID and VIC-II. They are negative features: slots cut into the tool, not separate ribs. Because they run across a thick section they leave visible flow lines and are a classic sink-mark site.

facts.label: Style
facts.value: through-slots, parallel to the long axis

facts.label: Function
facts.value: exhaust for the linear regulator and VIC/SID heat

children.note: The effectiveness of the case cooling was mediocre and reviewers noted heat trapping inside; the slots are modest.

children.name: Ribs and bosses behind the vent slots
children.description: Internal cross-ribs tying the top panel to the pan, moulded 1.5-2.5 mm thick at roughly the same gauge as the outer wall so the whole panel cools and shrinks as one. Where the ribs are thicker than the wall the extra melt freezes later and pulls a faint sink mark onto the visible surface.

facts.label: Design rule of thumb
facts.value: ribs capped at ~60% of the adjacent wall thickness

children.note: Mould-flow validation was in 1982 done by filling a clear polycarbonate or unfilled-PS prototype tool and watching flow fronts by eye or on a strobe, long before the widespread use of short-shot first-article reports.

children.name: Moulded bosses and standoffs
children.description: Integral cylindrical bosses on the pan floor that carry the four case screws, the motherboard mounting screws, the keyboard PCB screws and the RF shield tabs. Each is a thick section relative to the 3 mm pan, so the tool must be cored or cored-and-gauged to keep them from sinking, and each has a blind hole with a drafted self-tapping thread.

facts.label: Screw size
facts.value: 3 x 12 self-tapping into 6 mm OD bosses

facts.label: Boss bore
facts.value: ~2.5 mm with a shallow helix rib

children.name: Self-tapping thread form in plastic
children.description: A 1980s cost trick: instead of a moulded-in metal insert, the boss is cored with a shallow single-start helical flute of the same nominal diameter as a self-tapping screw. The screw's flank cuts its own thread on first insertion, giving a metal-in-plastic thread that will not strip.

facts.label: Cycle to first screw-in
facts.value: ~1 s at 1200 rpm on a hand screwdriver

facts.label: Serviceability
facts.value: poor; repeated removal strips the plastic

children.note: Commodore's later repro cases replace these with moulded-in brass inserts precisely because the self-tapping bosses break.

children.name: Rear and side connector openings
children.description: Rectangular and keyed cut-outs for the cartridge port, user port, cassette port, serial port, video DIN, power DIN and the two DE-9 control ports. Cut with knife-edged steel on the tool; the moulded lip around each port also acts as a draft and a finger stop, and the mouldings carry the connector bodies as separate inserts.

children.name: Front bezel (top half)
children.description: The dished front panel with the keyboard window. It is the visible part of the machine, so it carries the fine leather-grain texture, the rainbow badge recess, the two knurled thumbscrews and the moulded-in 'COMMODORE' lettering on the lower lip.

facts.label: Texture
facts.value: fine stochastic leather/pebble grain, depth 0.05-0.15 mm

facts.label: Screws to rear shell
facts.value: 6 self-tapping, plus 2 at the rear lip

children.name: Keyboard window and key openings
children.description: A single rectangular opening spanned by thin webs between the key holes; the caps push through and their plungers sit on the keyboard PCB below. The webs are the highest-risk area of the tool for short shots and flash, because the melt has to snake between 66 holes that are only about 10 mm across.

facts.label: Flash tolerance
facts.value: <0.2 mm, visually rejected at final inspection

children.note: Whether the bezel was a single moulding with the key openings, or a bezel with a separate keyboard frame, varies between breadbin tooling generations. Photographs of ASSY 250407 show one piece.

children.name: Moulded-in leather grain
children.description: The fine random pebble texture on the visible faces of the bezel and the rear shell. It is cut into the hardened tool steel by EDM from a positive pattern, then the whole cavity is polished and chrome-plated so the grain reads as a soft satin rather than as sharp metal. On genuine surviving Commodore tooling the flow pattern beneath the texture is still faintly visible, which is how restorers authenticate an original mould.

facts.label: Cut by
facts.value: EDM from a graphite or brass electrode

children.note: The texture is not paint or a coating: it is a negative in the steel. On parts made in a second colour or with a coating it can be partly buried, which is why grey aftermarket cases often look so much cleaner than originals.

children.name: Knurled thumbscrews for contrast/brightness
children.description: Two moulded plastic thumbscrews on the bezel that carry small metal shafts to the contrast and brightness potentiometers on the board. The caps are ABS, the shafts are plated steel, and the knurl is moulded rather than cut.
children.note: On some breadbin boards the potentiometers were adjusted by reaching into the case with a screwdriver and the two bezel thumbscrews only appear on later board revisions; check the specific assembly.

children.name: Rainbow Commodore badge
children.description: The seven-bar rainbow 'commodore' logo on the bezel. On the breadbin it is a raised area of the case itself, decorated by a run of coloured and metallised ink rather than being a separate appliqué; on later machines it is a flat printed decal.
children.note: Replicas, second-hand cases and modern reproductions disagree about whether the badge is raised mould or a bonded medallion. Surviving originals show a raised pad-printed area with the ink sitting in the texture; this is the most likely reading.

children.name: Raised badge area on the bezel
children.description: A shallow raised island on the bezel where the logo sits, moulded as part of the bezel tool. It gives the pad printer a flat, non-textured island so the ink sits proud of the leather grain and the colours read cleanly.

children.name: Case feet
children.description: Four small anti-vibration feet on the underside of the rear shell, moulded in a soft dark rubber or a flexible PVC, that stop the machine skating on a desk and stop the moulded ABS case from ringing against the desk.

facts.label: Typical material
facts.value: black styrene-butadiene rubber or soft PVC, insert-moulded or pressed in

children.note: Whether the C64 feet are insert-moulded SBR or simply flexible moulded-in stubs varies between units and I could not confirm the exact compound. Modern restorers often replace them with stick-on silicone bumpers, which suggests the originals were not always reliable.

children.name: Foot elastomer compound
children.description: A soft, low-durometer elastomer drop-in-moulded over a small ABS boss, or a moulded-in flexible nub. The chemistry is trivial but the tooling is not: it is a two-shot or insert-mould operation with an elastomer barrel and a much longer cure than the ABS.
children.note: Reuses the same butadiene and styrene monomers as the ABS and the SBR, which is a nice reminder that all four plastics in this machine trace back to the same steam cracker.

children.name: RFI shield: aluminium foil on a board spacer
children.description: The C64 needed a conductive screen over the motherboard because a 1 MHz machine with a video oscillator radiates through a plastic case. Commodore used a die-cut sandwich of aluminium foil laminated to a cardboard or plastic-fibre spacer, bent into a box and stapled or taped to plastic standoffs, rather than a full metal can.

facts.label: Spacer
facts.value: thin cardboard / greyboard, sometimes a plastic-fibre core

facts.label: Attachment
facts.value: stapled or taped to moulded plastic standoffs on the case floor

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: reduce RF radiation and ingress without a metal chassis

children.note: Retroleum catalogues three distinct breadbin foil-shield types (Types 1, 2 and 5) which tells you the shape was not standardised across the production run. Later boards (250425) got a stamped metal shield/heatsink that doubled as a cooler for the linear regulators.

children.name: Aluminium foil
children.description: Household or semi-rugged aluminium foil, 0.03-0.06 mm, slit and die-cut. Its job is not to be a Faraday cage in the strict sense but simply to be a continuous, grounded-ish conductor over the board so the radiated field collapses.
children.note: Household foil works surprisingly well for this, which is why computer makers scavenged it off consumer rolls. It tears easily, so the real difficulty is handling, not the material.

children.name: Aluminium slab casting and rolling
children.description: Bauxite is refined to alumina, smelted to primary aluminium in a Hall-Heroult potline at 950 C, then cast into rolling ingots and hot-rolled to foil gauge. Foil rolling is astonishingly aggressive: a 600 mm slab becomes 0.006 mm sheet after thousands of reduction passes.

facts.label: Carbon anode consumption
facts.value: ~1.2 t CO2 per tonne of aluminium

children.name: Shield spacer (board core)
children.description: A rigidising core so the foil does not crumple and short against the board. Cheap versions use thin greyboard; better ones use a plastic-fibre or corrugated spacer. This is the part that makes the shield stand off the motherboard so it cannot touch solder joints.
children.note: Board core is a plausible choice because the shield only needs to hold a shape and take handling, and greyboard is the cheapest stiff sheet in existence. Stamped sheet-metal shields were the alternative on later boards.

children.name: Case fasteners
children.description: The screws that hold the C64 together: a handful of case-assembly screws plus the motherboard and keyboard mounting screws. They are cheap zinc-plated self-tapping screws into plastic bosses, with occasional brass inserts.

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: zinc or nickel-zinc, plus a nylon patch for vibration

children.note: The common failure mode of a forty-year-old C64 is a snapped screw boss, not a rusted screw. Repro cases now mould in brass inserts to fix exactly this.

children.name: Cold heading and thread cutting
children.description: Steel wire is drawn, cut to length, cold-headed on a multiple-spindle header, the thread is cut or rolled, and the head is slotted or Phillips-formed. This is one of the most automated manufacturing processes on earth: a header makes tens of thousands of screws an hour with essentially no machining.

facts.label: Thread
facts.value: cut or rolled; rolled threads are stronger

children.name: Zinc electroplating of fasteners
children.description: Small parts are barrel-plated in an acid or alkaline zinc solution, then often chromate-passivated for corrosion resistance. Zinc is chosen because it is sacrificial and cheap, and because a partly-depleted zinc coat on a thirty-year-old screw looks like rust rather than like a defect.

facts.label: Passivation
facts.value: yellow or clear chromate conversion coat

children.name: Moulded-in brass insert (later practice)
children.description: Modern repro cases and late Commodore tools mould a brass or stainless insert into the boss and use a real machine screw. The insert is placed by hand or by gravity feed and captured by the ABS on the next shot, giving a reusable metal thread.
children.note: Original 1982 breadbins used self-tapping screws into plain plastic bosses. Inserts are the later improvement.

children.name: ABS resin, general-purpose injection grade
children.description: Acrylonitrile-butadiene-styrene: a SAN matrix rigidified by acrylonitrile, toughened by grafted polybutadiene and given surface gloss by styrene. Commodore bought commodity ABS pellets in 25 kg bags, compounded them with colour masterbatch in a merchant compounder, and shipped them to case factories in Hong Kong and Taiwan.
children.note: A textured housing wants a LOW rubber content. High-rubber grades flow better but leave a soft, smeared grain; housing grades are typically chosen for a stiff, sharp texture and low sink.

children.name: Emulsion graft polymerisation to ABS
children.description: The dominant ABS route since the 1960s and still the one that makes the resin in the C64. Butadiene is polymerised in water to a polybutadiene latex; styrene and acrylonitrile are graft-polymerised onto that latex; the graft latex is coagulated, dewatered, dried and compounded with separately made bulk-SAN resin.

facts.label: Initiation
facts.value: potassium or sodium persulfate, or an organic persulfate

facts.label: Residual monomer removal
facts.value: steam stripping in a vacuum plate column

children.name: Monomer triad fed to the ABS plant
children.description: Styrene supplies gloss and mouldability, acrylonitrile supplies rigidity and chemical resistance, butadiene supplies the rubber phase that survives the drop the machine takes off a desk. All three arrive as cracker or reformer products, not as laboratory reagents.

children.name: Styrene monomer
children.description: Vinylbenzene, made by catalytic dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene or by styrene monomer recovery from a cracker. 1980s ABS plants bought it at 99.5%+ into stainless bulk tanks.

children.name: Ethylbenzene dehydrogenation to styrene
children.description: Endothermic vapour-phase dehydrogenation of ethylbenzene over shell-type alumina-iron catalysts at 600-700 C, giving styrene plus hydrogen. Modern plants add a styrene monomer recovery loop to recycle unreacted ethylbenzene; 1980s plants ran single-pass at roughly 50-60% conversion and burned the rest.
children.note: The styrene monomer recovery loop that pushes per-pass conversion to ~65-70% became mandatory in OECD plants after about 1990. 1982 ABS resin was typically made without it.

children.name: Ethylbenzene
children.description: Benzene alkylated with ethylene (or propylene) over a solid acid to make the styrene feedstock, with diethylbenzene and triethylbenzene as the by-products that have to be separated out.

children.name: Benzene alkylation with ethylene
children.description: Friedel-Crafts alkylation over amorphous silica-alumina or a zeolite at 200-350 C and 5-20 bar, giving ethylbenzene plus polyalkylated heavies removed by fractionation.

children.name: Benzene
children.description: A C6H6 aromatic produced either by catalytic reforming of naphtha or by hydrodealkylation of toluene. Benzene is the entry point to styrene, and via cumene to phenol, epoxy resin and polycarbonate.

children.name: Catalytic reforming and aromatics extraction
children.description: Naphtha is vaporised and passed over platinum (often with rhenium) on gamma-alumina at 450-520 C and 5-30 bar. Naphthenes and paraffins dehydrocyclise to aromatics; the C6+ aromatics are then split by extractive distillation with sulfolane or by azeotropic distillation with NMP.
children.note: Reformer pressure is the era tell. Low-pressure (5-10 bar) reformers dominate outside the US; semi-regenerative high-pressure units (15-30 bar) were the standard US build in 1982; continuous catalyst regeneration only arrived in earnest in the mid-1980s.

children.name: Platinum-alumina reforming catalyst
children.description: 0.3-0.5 wt% platinum with rhenium, chloride and fluoride promoters dispersed on synthetic gamma-alumina. The platinum comes from PGM ores or from spent refinery catalyst; the alumina support is sintered from calcined bauxite.

children.name: Platinum-group metal concentrate
children.description: Sulfide ore mined in South Africa's Bushveld complex or Russia's Norilsk, concentrated and smelted to a matte, then leached and refined. The platinum fraction is a fraction of a percent of the ore, which is why reclaiming spent catalyst is a real industry.
children.note: Mine origin is generic. Also, note that the C64's own story and this ore are unrelated - the platinum is for the refinery, not the C64.

children.name: Bauxite (alumina precursor)
children.description: Hydrated alumina rock, mined and Bayer-refined to alumina. It is the source of the alumina support for the reforming catalyst, and also the ore that becomes the aluminium in the EMI shield.

children.name: Acrylonitrile (vinyl cyanide)
children.description: CH2=CH-CN, the polar monomer that gives ABS its rigidity and resistance to solvents. Almost all of it is made by catalytic ammoxidation of propylene with ammonia and air over a bismuth-molybdate catalyst in a fluidised bed.

children.name: Sovereign/BP ammoxidation of propylene
children.description: Propylene, ammonia and air are fed together into a turbulent fluidised-bed reactor over a bismuth-molybdate-on-silica catalyst at 400-510 C and only 1.5-3 bar. Acrylonitrile comes out together with acetonitrile, HCN and COx; the gases are quenched in a countercurrent water absorber, the AN is distilled, and the residual ammonia is neutralised with sulphuric acid to ammonium sulphate fertiliser.
children.note: Originally the Sohio (Standard Oil of Ohio) process, later sold by SOHIO to BP and rebranded 'Sovereign'. An older route, acetylene plus hydrogen cyanide, was still in use into the 1980s in a few plants but was being retired.

children.name: Ammonia
children.description: Made by steam-methane reforming natural gas to synthesis gas (CO+H2) and then Haber-Bosch synthesis over promoted iron. Every tonne of acrylonitrile needs roughly a quarter tonne of ammonia, and the byproduct ammonium sulphate goes straight back onto farmland.

children.name: Steam-methane reforming (primary reformer)
children.description: Natural gas and steam are burned over nickel at 800-900 C to give synthesis gas, CO plus H2. The high-temperature endothermic step is fired by burning part of the gas itself, so an ammonia plant is really a gas-fired furnace with a chemistry attached.

children.name: Haber-Bosch ammonia synthesis
children.description: Nitrogen and hydrogen react at 400-500 C and 150-300 bar over an iron catalyst promoted with K2O and Al2O3. This is where the era shows: 1980s plants ran the classic packed-bed, and modern plants use much more efficient ruthenium catalysts at lower pressure.
children.note: The switch from iron to ruthenium catalysts in the 1990s cut energy use per tonne of ammonia roughly in half. In 1982 it was all iron.

children.name: Bismuth phosphomolybdate ammoxidation catalyst
children.description: The heart of the ammoxidation. A mixture of bismuth, molybdenum, iron, cobalt and other metal oxides, typically supported on silica or silica-alumina. It works by a redox cycle: the lattice oxygen of the molybdate grabs an allylic hydrogen from propylene, ammonia inserts, the nitrile is desorbed, and air re-oxidises the bismuth.
children.note: The bismuth-molybdate family is one of the great success stories of heterogeneous catalysis: the same catalyst family is used for the ammoxidation to acrylonitrile, for acrolein to acrylic acid, and for the butadiene to butene oxide.

children.name: Bismuth ore and bismuth compounds
children.description: Bismuth comes mainly as a by-product of lead and copper refining, from bismuthinite (Bi2S3) or as native bismuth in tin/tungsten veins. The oxo-nitrate is precipitated from an acid solution and calcined to bismuth oxide for the catalyst.

children.name: Molybdenum ore (molybdenite)
children.description: Molybdenite, MoS2, mined mostly as a by-product of porphyry copper. It is roasted to technical-grade molybdic oxide and then purified to the high-purity metal or oxidised for catalyst use.

children.name: Silica / silica-alumina support
children.description: The porous carrier for the bismuth molybdate, made from diatomaceous earth or by co-precipitating silica from sodium silicate. Diatomaceous earth is a filter-aid mineral mined from ancient diatomite deposits.

children.name: Butadiene (1,3-butadiene)
children.description: The rubber monomer. 1980s butadiene came almost entirely from the C4 fraction of the steam cracker, extracted by extractive distillation (or by older acetylene-dimerisation routes still running in Europe).

children.name: Recovery of butadiene from the C4 cut
children.description: The C4 stream from the cracker contains butenes, isobutene and butadiene. Because butadiene boils at -4 C and its neighbours at +1 to +13 C, it is separated by extractive distillation with a heavy solvent such as NMP or furfural in a tall column, or by older acetonedimethylformamide absorption.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: extractive distillation (NMP/furfural) or older chemical absorption

facts.label: Challenge
facts.value: isomerise to 1,2-butene; polymerise in transit; high pressure

children.note: The older DDM (acetone/DMF) absorption-recovery route was still being phased out in the early 1980s; by the mid-1980s extractive distillation had won almost everywhere.

children.name: Steam cracking of naphtha (the source of all four monomers)
children.description: Naphtha or gas oil is vaporised, mixed with steam and flashed through coils in a radiant furnace at 800-900 C in a few tenths of a second. The gas is quenched fast to stop further cracking, then fractionated into hydrogen, ethylene, propylene, a C4 cut and an aromatics cut. Almost every polymer in the C64 - ABS, SAN, SBR feet, polystyrene foam - starts as a cut out of this one column.
children.note: Modern crackers push higher severity (coils to 950-1000 C) and use more structured/elliptical coils. In 1982 the classic coiled-pipe radiant furnace was still the workhorse. The coils themselves were cast from a 25/35 nickel alloy, which is a real and expensive material choice because the coking rate falls exponentially with nickel.

children.name: Cracker coil casting in high-nickel alloy
children.description: Radiant furnace coils are investment-cast from HK40 or 35Cr-45Ni alloy in twenty to forty segments, then thermally expanded into the tube supports. The nickel content is what keeps the coil from coking and creeping at 850 C.

children.name: Refractory fibre block lining
children.description: The furnace interior is lined with castable alumina and calcium-aluminate refractory or ceramic fibre blanket to hold 850 C and survive thermal cycling. It is a consumable and a real maintenance cost.

children.name: Emulsifier (fatty-acid soap)
children.description: The ABS latex is not made with a synthetic surfactant but with cheap soap - typically a sodium or potassium salt of a C16-C18 fatty acid, sometimes blended with a sulfosuccinate for stability. This is the 1980s process: fully synthetic surfactants were still expensive.

facts.label: Typical emulsifier
facts.value: sodium oleate / potassium oleate, or an alkylbenzenesulfonate

children.note: Emulsifier choice has a big effect on the final particle size, and particle size is what sets the impact toughness. Producers who got it wrong had to agglomerate the latex or add a second, more expensive surfactant.

children.name: Free-radical initiator (persulfate)
children.description: Potassium persulfate or sodium persulfate, thermally decomposed in the aqueous reactor to start the radical chain. Cheap, and the resulting sulphate is later washed out during coagulation.

children.name: Potassium hydroxide (caustic potash)
children.description: Made by chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine, the potassium salt crystallising from the sodium-rich liquor. It is what turns the fatty acid into the soap emulsifier and the persulfate precursor into the initiator.

children.name: Chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine
children.description: Electrolysis of saturated brine in a membrane or mercury cell splits salt water into chlorine, sodium (or potassium) hydroxide and hydrogen. This is one of the foundational 20th-century chemical processes and it feeds PVC, solvents, and every chlorinated intermediate.

facts.label: Cell type (1980s)
facts.value: diaphragm, mercury or membrane; membrane gaining share by mid-1980s

facts.label: Voltage
facts.value: ~3 V per cell, but 100-150 V across a cell house

children.note: Mercury-cell electrolysis was still the dominant technology in 1982, but was being phased out over environmental and product-quality reasons in favour of the membrane cell. This transition is one of the clean examples of where 1980s practice differs from modern practice.

children.name: Halite (rock salt)
children.description: Sodium chloride, mined or solution-mined from evaporite deposits and dissolved to make the brine that is electrolysed. Pure salt is the raw material for the entire chlor-alkali chemical complex.

children.name: SAN resin (styrene-acrylonitrile) matrix component
children.description: Most ABS is a blend: grafted rubber plus a separately polymerised SAN. The SAN is the continuous, glossy, rigid phase; the grafted rubber is the dispersed, toughening phase. The SAN is usually made by bulk or emulsion polymerisation in a separate plant and shipped to the ABS compounding line as pellets or as latex.

facts.label: Typical AN content in the SAN
Share of SAN in the finished ABS

children.name: Bulk polymerisation of SAN (plug flow)
children.description: A monomer mixture of styrene and acrylonitrile is polymerised thermally in a series of stirred, jacketed plug-flow reactors - classic 'prepolymerise then finish' with the reactor temperature ramped from ~130 C to ~230 C to convert 95-99% of the monomer. The SAN is devolatilised and extruded to pellets.

children.name: Additives package added at compounding
children.description: ABS pellets as delivered are a straw-coloured, unpigmented polymer. The beige-brown of the C64 case is added downstream at the compounder as a colour masterbatch, along with stabilisers, a release agent and, in some grades, a flame retardant. A 1982 C64 case is almost certainly pigmented at the compound line, not at the moulder.
children.note: The brown-to-blonde colour shift over forty years is the classic ABS photodegradation: the butadiene rubber phase oxidises at the surface and the whole part browns uniformly. UV stabiliser and pigment loading both affect how fast it happens.

children.name: Pigment masterbatch (colour concentrate)
children.description: A high-loading pellet of pigment dispersed in an ABS or PE carrier resin, let down at 1-4% into the natural ABS. The colour masterbatch is itself a compounding product, made on its own twin-screw line.

facts.label: Carrier
facts.value: ABS or PE, matched to base for colour

children.name: Phthalocyanine blue pigment
children.description: Copper phthalocyanine (PB15), an intensely coloured, heat-stable, lightfast blue used for the cool grey-blue tones on some cases. Copper plus four phthalonitrile rings, assembled in a violent exotherm.

children.name: Phthalic anhydride
children.description: Made by air oxidation of o-xylene over vanadia-titania catalysts at ~450 C. It is the classic route to phthalocyanine pigments and to glycidyl ester epoxy resins.

children.name: o-Xylene
children.description: One of the three xylene isomers separated out of the mixed aromatics from the reformer by adsorption (UOP Parex-type) or by distillation. The ortho isomer is the one that gets oxidised to phthalic anhydride.
children.note: The separation of the isomers by molecular adsorption (Parex/UOP) is a good example of 1980s petrochemical sophistication: the unit separates individual isomers from the C8 cut on a zeolite molecular sieve.

children.name: C8 aromatics separation (UOP Parex)
children.description: Para-xylene is selectively adsorbed from the mixed C8 aromatics onto a zeolite molecular sieve, desorbed with a purge, leaving o- and m-xylene. It is a swinging adsorption unit with hundreds of adsorbent beds and rotating valves.

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: mixed C8 aromatics from the reformer

children.note: Parex-type units date from 1962 and were ubiquitous in 1982 for making terephthalic acid (PET). Modern units use improved adsorbents but the process is essentially unchanged.

children.name: Copper for the phthalocyanine centre
children.description: Copper(II) salts, from electrorefined copper. Copper comes from chalcopyrite CuFeS2 ore or from ore sorted to a copper concentrate, then smelted, converted and electrorefined.

children.name: Chalcopyrite (copper ore)
children.description: CuFeS2, the dominant copper ore, mined underground or in large open pits and concentrated by flotation before smelting. The smelter's job is to strip the iron into slag so that copper matte can be converted and electrorefined.

children.name: Froth flotation of copper ore
children.description: Crushed and ground ore is conditioned with xanthate collectors and frothers, and the copper sulfide particles are floated to the surface in a bank of rectangular flotation cells. This is how most of the world's copper is separated from its host rock.

facts.label: Cells
facts.value: dozens in series, each a few m3

children.name: Flash smelting and converting
children.description: Sulfide concentrate is blown with oxygen-enriched air in a flash furnace at ~1250 C, so that the sulfur burns and autogenous heat smelts the copper. The resulting matte is oxidised in converters, slagged of its iron, and the blister copper is electrorefined.

children.name: Titanium dioxide (white pigment)
children.description: The workhorse white pigment, present in almost every beige or grey ABS and in most white packaging ink. Rutile is the industrial grade: made by chlorinating ilmenite or rutile ore to TiCl4, then oxidising it in a 1000 C flame to pure white rutile pigment.

children.name: Ilmenite and rutile ore
children.description: Titanium ore, mined from beach sands and hard-rock deposits. Ilmenite (FeTiO3) is the dominant feed; it is reduced to titanium slag, or chlorinated to TiCl4.
children.note: Beach-sand ilmenite and rutile are dredged or wet-separated; the heavy-mineral concentrate then goes to a chlorinator. This is one of the clearest 'ore -> pigment -> plastic case' chains on the machine.

children.name: Metallurgical coke
children.description: The reductant in the chlorinator (TiO2 + 2C + 2Cl2 -> TiCl4 + 2CO) and the fuel of the flame reactor. Coke is a by-product of coking coal in a coke oven battery, not a mined material in itself.
children.note: Coking coal is thermal-rank coal (bituminous), chosen for its caking properties. The coke oven itself is one of the great carbon-emitting industrial plants of the period.

children.name: Release agent / lubricant
children.description: A trace of an internal lubricant such as a metal stearate (zinc or calcium stearate, or a fatty-acid ester) is compounded into the ABS so the mould releases cleanly. Too much and it bloats the surface of the textured area.

children.name: Stearic acid
children.description: C18 saturated fatty acid, made by hydrogenating tallow (or palm stearin) or by pressing stearic acid out of beef tallow. It is the base of the metal stearate lubricants and also of many cosmetic-grade waxes.

facts.label: Typical source
facts.value: hydrogenated palm stearin or beef tallow

children.note: Tallow is rendered animal fat - itself a byproduct of the meat industry. Palm stearin is the fraction of palm oil that solidifies. Both are agricultural, not petrochemical, feedstocks.

children.name: Tallow (rendered fat)
children.description: Rendered bovine or ovine fat, a slaughterhouse byproduct, used historically as a soap and lubricant feedstock and as a fatty-acid source.

children.name: Flame retardant additive (optional)
children.description: Not all ABS is flame retardant, but electronics housings were often specified with a UL94 HB or V-2 grade, which is achieved by adding a halogenated additive - typically brominated epoxy or an aliphatic bromine-chlorine compound at 5-15 parts per hundred. It slows burning but costs toughness and colour, so a textured beige housing usually avoided it.

facts.label: Common systems
facts.value: brominated epoxy resin, or chlorinated paraffin

facts.label: Cost
facts.value: raises cost and lowers Izod impact, so it is usually a trade

children.note: For a home computer case a flame-retardant grade is a 'nice to have' rather than a requirement; household-computable housings of 1982 were commonly general-purpose ABS. Included because flame retardants were a standard part of the 1980s ABS additive package.

children.name: Twin-screw compounding and pelletising
children.description: Natural ABS pellets are let down with the colour masterbatch and additives on a co-rotating twin-screw extruder, degassed, filtered through a screen pack, and pelletised - chopped strands or underwater cut. This is a 1980s standard plastic-compounding line.

facts.label: Throughput (merchant line)
facts.value: a few hundred kg/h to 1-2 t/h

children.note: In the 1980s screen-pack melt filtration and gravimetric dosing were the state of the art; modern lines add online viscometers and inline colour measurement, but the twin-screw itself has not fundamentally changed.

children.name: Case tooling: H13 family mould with EDM texture
children.description: The two breadbin case moulds are large two-plate tools in pre-hardened or hardened hot-work steel, with the leather-grain texture cut by electrical discharge machining and the cavity polished and hard-chromed. A single mould produces thousands of C64 cases; its cost is amortised over millions of parts, so Commodore could afford a 5-cavity family tool.

facts.label: Tool size
facts.value: ~450 x 350 mm, two-plate, guided by leader pins

facts.label: Cavities
facts.value: typically 1 large cavity for a case this size; 2-4 on smaller tools

facts.label: Nickel content of plating
facts.value: hard chrome, or electroless nickel of ~5-10 um

facts.label: Tool life by run size
facts.value: large ABS housing tool 300,000-1,000,000+ shots with periodic rebuild; small high-cavity keycap tool similar; short-run and prototype tools may only see 30,000-200,000

children.note: A household-computer case is a big, shallow, textured tool - about as hard a mould as 1982 injection moulding got. Chrome plating of the cavity is what makes the texture read as a soft satin and is also what gives tool life: the chrome is harder than the polished steel and takes the abrasion of millions of shots. A C64 case was needed in the tens of millions, so a single tool had to survive tens of millions of shots or be rebuilt several times; that economics is why the tool is chrome-plated and maintained rather than run to failure.

children.name: Tool steel (P20 pre-hardened or H13/SKD61 hardened)
children.description: Most 1980s housing tools were cut from pre-hardened P20-type steel (about HRC 30-35) so the tool could be finished-machined without distortion. Tools needing more polish cycles or more heat went to H13/SKD61, vacuum-hardened and tempered to HRC 44-50.
children.note: Which grade Commodore actually used for the breadbin tooling I could not confirm; P20-class and H13-class were both routine for a case of this size in 1982.

children.name: H13 / SKD61 hot-work tool steel
children.description: A 5% Cr, 1% Mo, 1% V, 0.4% C alloy. Chromium gives hardenability and polishability, molybdenum and vanadium give secondary hardness and temper resistance. Also sold as DIN X40CrMoV5-1, JIS SKD61 or AISI H13.

facts.label: Critical for tools
facts.value: deep hardening plus temper resistance near 250-300 C

children.name: Ferrochrome from chromite ore
children.description: Chromite, FeCr2O4, is smelted in a submerged-arc or submerged-top furnace with coke and lime to give high-carbon ferrochrome, then refined to low-carbon ferrochrome. Almost all the chromium in a tool steel charge comes in as ferrochrome.

facts.label: Smelting
facts.value: s submerged-arc furnace with coke, 1500-1700 C

children.name: Chromite ore
children.description: The only economic chromium ore, mined mostly in South Africa's Bushveld complex and in Zimbabwe, Kazakhstan and Turkey. Sold as a lumpy or sintered lump, or as a fines fraction.

children.name: Ferromolybdenum from molybdite
children.description: Molybdenite is roasted to technical molybdic oxide (MoO3) and then reduced with aluminium or in a submerged-arc furnace with coke to ferromolybdenum, which is dosed into the steel melt.

facts.label: Roasting
facts.value: 600-700 C, 2-4 h in a multiple-hearth furnace

children.name: Ferrovanadium from vanadiferous slag
children.description: Vanadium is not mined as a vanadium ore at all in most of the world. It is recovered as a byproduct: vanadiferous titanomagnetite slag from iron ore smelting is re-smelted, or slag is leached with soda ash, and vanadium is precipitated and reduced to ferrovanadium.

facts.label: Main route
facts.value: byproduct of iron ore smelting (vanadiferous titanomagnetite)

facts.label: Leach
facts.value: soda ash / salt roasting then aqueous leach

children.note: The vanadium in a tool steel therefore traces back to an iron ore blast furnace, not to a vanadium mine. A nice non-obvious ore-to-tool chain.

children.name: Iron ore (vanadiferous magnetite)
children.description: The ore is smelted in a blast furnace; when it carries vanadium the slag is deliberately kept for vanadium recovery. So the same lump of ore yields the iron for the press frame and, later, the vanadium in the tool steel.
children.note: Blast furnace coke is made from coking coal in a coke oven battery; the limestone flux is quarried.

children.name: Vacuum hardening and tempering of the tool
children.description: H13 is austenitised at 1000-1050 C, quenched in air or in vacuum, then double-tempered at 500-600 C to get secondary hardness. Vacuum is preferred because it avoids decarburisation and the distortion that salt baths cause. In 1982 salt baths were still very common for smaller tools.

facts.label: Quench
facts.value: air or vacuum; salt bath (550 C) was the 1970s norm

children.note: Modern tooling shops would use a fine-grain, high-purity steel and a tighter hardness window; 1982 practice was adequate but variable, and the variation is exactly why some original C64 cases show a slightly different gloss.

children.name: Nitriding of the polished cavity
children.description: A short nitriding treatment after polishing diffuses nitrogen into the surface, growing a hard, low-friction skin on the cavity that resists the corrosive effect of styrene monomer. Standard on hot-runner tools and increasingly used on ABS housings.

children.name: P20 pre-hardened tool steel
children.description: A 0.38% C, 0.9% Cr, 0.4% Mo, 0.2% V steel supplied at HRC 30-35. Because it arrives hard, the whole cavity can be machined and polished with no risk of distortion from a later heat treatment, which is why it dominated housing tooling in 1982.

facts.label: Trade names
facts.value: P20, 1.2311, NAK80 is the corrosion-resistant modern cousin

children.note: The mould texturing and polishing described below works equally on P20 or on H13.

children.name: Machining of the cavity and core
children.description: A 1982 tool shop would rough the cavity with large carbide or HSS milling cutters, leaving 0.3-0.5 mm, then finish-mill, then grind the critical faces flat and parallel, then EDM the texture, then lap and polish. Rough and finish were both done on machining centres or on conventional mills and grinders - CNC was normal but not universal.
children.note: By 1982 CNC machining centres and CNC grinders were standard in Taiwanese and Hong Kong tool shops, so this is genuinely a CNC-era tool even though the process sequence is unchanged.

children.name: Surface grinding and the parting line
children.description: The two plates are ground parallel and the parting plane is lapped. A visible flash line around the case seam is the parting line: on a housing tool it is put exactly at the joint line of the two halves so it disappears into the joint.

children.name: EDM cutting of the leather grain
children.description: The texture is the one feature that cannot be milled: a random stochastic pattern of overlapping spherical dimples. It is cut by sinking a shaped graphite or brass electrode into the hardened, ground cavity, or by wire-EDM scanning. Sinking EDM gives a whole panel at once; wire EDM gives resolution but is slower.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: sinker (sink) EDM is standard for area texturing; wire EDM for detail

facts.label: Electrode
facts.value: graphite, or brass for finer detail

facts.label: Rough cut
facts.value: ~0.2-0.5 mm/s removal; finish cut much slower

children.note: Sinker EDM existed and was well established by 1982 - it had been commercial since the 1960s - so the texture is genuinely of its period. What has NOT changed is that the texture is a negative in the steel, not a coating.

children.name: Graphite electrode for EDM texturing
children.description: Isostatic-pressed fine-grain graphite, turned or milled to the negative of the texture panel, or a CNC-shaped graphite block. Graphite is used because it is easy to machine, wears predictably as the electrode erodes, and does not damage the workpiece the way a metal electrode would.

children.name: Natural graphite flake
children.description: Flake graphite is mined in Sri Lanka, Madagascar, China and Brazil, purified by acid (or in the 1980s by chlorination) and pressed with pitch binder into tooling graphite.
children.note: China was the dominant supplier of graphite electrode and tooling graphite throughout this period.

children.name: Brass electrode for fine detail
children.description: Copper-zinc alloy electrodes are used where the texture has fine features, because brass machines more accurately than graphite and can be reworked. Brass comes from copper and zinc ores smelted together.

children.name: Lapping and polishing the cavity
children.description: The cavity is progressively polished - progressively finer abrasives on cloth and stone - to a mirror. On a textured tool the polish is done to the whole surface and the texture simply stays; on flat surfaces it goes to Ra 0.05-0.1 um, which is what makes the plated ABS read as glossy.

facts.label: Polishing media
facts.value: aluminium oxide, then chromium oxide for the final mirror

facts.label: Hand vs machine
facts.value: hand polishing on cast iron blocks for the final mirror; machine polish for bulk stock removal

children.note: This is the most labour-intensive step in the whole case tool. A large textured housing cavity takes days of hand polishing, which is why such tools cost tens of thousands of dollars and why the economics demanded millions of parts.

children.name: Abrasive polishing compounds
children.description: Aluminium oxide for the bulk work, green chromium oxide for the final mirror. Both are made from bauxite or from chromite.

children.name: Synthetic alumina abrasive
children.description: Bauxite is refined to alumina and sintered or fused into corundum, then crushed and graded into abrasive powders. Hardness ~9 on the Mohs scale, second only to diamond, and the workhorse of metal finishing.

children.name: Hard chrome plating of the cavity
children.description: The polished cavity is electroplated in a hexavalent chromium bath to a few microns. Chrome is much harder than the tool steel, so the tool wears far better; it is also what gives the moulded ABS its character - the gloss of a C64 case is the gloss of chrome, not of steel.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: chromic acid with sulfate catalyst, 50-60 C, 6-10 V

facts.label: Hydrogen embrittlement
facts.value: a real risk; many moulds are baked immediately after plating

facts.label: Environmental cost
facts.value: Cr(VI) plating is heavily restricted today

children.note: Modern practice has largely moved away from hexavalent chromium for environmental reasons, toward electroless nickel or PVD. In 1982 hard chrome was the standard and there was no practical alternative.

children.name: Chromic acid for the plating bath
children.description: Made by roasting chromite with soda ash and limestone, leaching the sodium chromate, and acidifying. So the chromium in the plating bath comes from the same chromite that came into the tool steel.

facts.label: Roasting
facts.value: ~1000 C with soda ash and lime, oxidative roast to Na2CrO4

children.note: Chromium plating is one of the few places the same ore appears twice in a single product: once as alloying element in the steel, once as the surface plating.

children.name: Mould assembly: guide pins, ejectors, cooling
children.description: The finished plates are set into a mould base with guide pillars or bushes, an ejector-plate assembly with pins under every feature that would imprint on the visible face, and water lines carrying coolant through the cores and plates to remove the heat of plasticisation.

facts.label: Cooling
facts.value: water at 30-60 C through baffles and core channels

facts.label: Hot runner
facts.value: unusual on a large ABS housing tool in 1982; cold runner with a pressure-controlled gate was normal

children.note: Hot-runner tools avoid the runner itself as scrap but were expensive and finicky; for a big low-volume-per-cavity housing the cold runner was simply cheaper, and the runner was ground up and recycled.

children.name: Injection moulding of the case
children.description: The bezel and rear shell are moulded on a large toggle or hydraulic press in a multi-cavity family tool. The ABS is dried, melted at around 250 C, injected at high pressure through a gate on the parting line, cooled against water channels, and ejected with pin marks and a visible gate vestige.

facts.label: Press clamp force
facts.value: 300-600 t (C64 case is a wide but shallow tool)

facts.label: Cycle time
facts.value: 30-60 s for a case this size

facts.label: ABS shrinkage
facts.value: 0.4-0.7%, so the tool is made oversize

children.note: A C64 case is a large, thin, textured part - the hardest kind of thing to mould without flow marks or short shots. The mould temperature control is what decides whether the leather grain comes out crisp or smeared. Note on wall thickness: a C64 case is a thin-walled part at roughly 2.5-3.5 mm, not the 6-8 mm quoted for thick structural mouldings - which is exactly why it is prone to flow marks and short shots.

children.name: Injection press (300-600 t)
children.description: A toggle or direct-hydraulic injection moulding machine with a screw plasticiser, a heated barrel with three or four zones, an oil or water temperature controller, and a mould base. Toggle machines clamp faster and are what most housing tools ran on.

children.name: Plasticising screw and barrel
children.description: A flighted screw turns in a heated barrel, conveying and melting pellets on the way back and injecting on the way forward. The screw is nitrided 33CrMoV or 40Cr steel, bimetallic-lined at the tip in later designs.

facts.label: Diameter
facts.value: typically 25-40 mm L/D 20-28 for this shot size

children.name: Hydraulic clamp unit
children.description: Oil hydraulics drive the toggle or the platen, provide injection and holding pressure, and drive the ejector. A hydraulic press is the reason injection pressure reached 1000+ bar - compared with the ~500 bar of the older toggle-and-screw machines.
children.note: This is a mechanical node rather than a chemical one, but the press is capital equipment that traces back to cast iron, cast steel and oil.

children.name: Drying the ABS before moulding
children.description: ABS is hygroscopic: even a little absorbed water hydrolyses the nitrile groups at melt temperature, causing splay streaks and reduced molecular weight. Pellets are dried before use - typically 2-4 hours at 80-90 C in a hot-air, dehumidifying hopper dryer - to below about 0.05% moisture.

facts.label: Failure mode
facts.value: silver streaks (splay) on the visible surface

children.note: ABS is not as moisture-sensitive as polycarbonate or PET, but 1982 practice was to dry it anyway for textured visible parts. In 1982 the dryer was usually a simple hot-air hopper with a molecular-sieve or silica-gel desiccant, not the closed-loop dehumidifying type that became normal in the 1990s.

children.name: Desiccant for the drying hopper
children.description: Either silica gel or, better, a synthetic zeolite molecular sieve (3A/4A) that adsorbs water at low partial pressure and regenerates at 200-300 C. Zeolites are made from kaolin or from amorphous silica and alumina.

children.name: Kaolin (china clay)
children.description: A white clay, essentially kaolinite Al2Si2O5(OH)4, washed from a kaolin pit, calcined and reacted with sodium aluminate or caustic to make a 4A zeolite molecular sieve. Kaolin is a dug mineral, not a petrochemical.

children.name: Melting and plasticising the ABS
children.description: The screw melts and homogenises the pellets as it retracts. Back pressure and screw speed set the melt temperature. For ABS the barrel zones run roughly 200 (feed) to 250-260 C (nozzle); the melt must be well above the 100 C Vicat softening point but below the ~270 C where ABS starts to degrade.

facts.label: Screw speed
facts.value: 20-60 rpm typical; higher speed increases shear heat

facts.label: Residence time
facts.value: keep under ~10 min to avoid thermal degradation

children.note: ABS is comparatively forgiving to process - unlike polycarbonate, which has to be kept dry and under 290 C - which is one reason it won home-computer housings.

children.name: Injection and packing under pressure
children.description: The mould is closed, the screw drives forward and the melt is forced into the cavity through the gate at high pressure, then held under pressure to pack the part to full density and to control sink marks. The pressure must exceed the pressure drop along the flow path, so thin, long, textured flows need very high injection pressure - this is why C64 cases show flow marks (the '2-point flow pattern' that Commodore's revived tooling still carries).

facts.label: Gate
facts.value: edge gate or a small sprue on the parting line

facts.label: Pack pressure
facts.value: 50-100 bar held while the gate is frozen

facts.label: Cavity fill
facts.value: must be full within a second or the ABS cools and frosts

children.note: The visible 'flow marks' or 'weld line' on a C64 case is the frozen boundary between two melt fronts that met and did not fully knit - the two-point pattern is that boundary, now preserved as part of the tool's signature.

children.name: Cooling and controlled crystallisation
children.description: The mould is water-cooled, or temperature-controlled, and the part is held until it has shrunk to the tool dimension. Cooling is the dominant term in the cycle time for a large ABS housing, and controlling the rate matters as much as the total: cool too fast on one side and the part distorts; too slow and the cycle stretches.

facts.label: Cooling time
facts.value: 20-40 s (major part of the 30-60 s cycle)

facts.label: Shrinkage on cooling
facts.value: 0.4-0.7% linear, so the tool cavity is cut oversize

children.note: Because ABS shrinks 0.4-0.7% with cooling, every dimension in the tool has to be compensated; for the key openings this is why caps fit but the plastic web between them is always slightly thinner than the drawing.

children.name: Ejection, pin marks and gate vestige
children.description: Ejector pins push the part off the core and off the gate. They leave small round marks, usually inside the case where nobody sees them. The gate leaves a small scar on the parting line that is trimmed or simply hidden by the two halves of the case meeting over it.

facts.label: Gate vestige
facts.value: a small disc or gate-cut scar on the parting line

facts.label: Parting line
facts.value: a faint hairline around the seam where the two halves meet

children.note: The parting line, the gate vestige and the ejector pin marks are the fingerprints that prove a case was injection-moulded rather than vacuum-formed or 3D-printed - useful to anyone trying to date a case.

children.name: Insert moulding of metal and plastic fittings
children.description: Things that cannot be moulded in - metal shields, posts, threads - are placed in the cavity before the shot and over-moulded. In a C64 case the shield standoffs and sometimes threaded metal inserts are insert-moulded this way.

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: by hand or gravity feed on a fast cycle

facts.label: Used for
facts.value: brass inserts, shield standoffs, key guides

children.name: Multi-shot / two-colour moulding
children.description: A second shot in a second cavity moulds a second colour or material over the first, giving a hard-wearing colour layer or a soft-touch overmould. The technique existed and was used in 1982, but the breadbin case is essentially a single-colour ABS shell: the colour comes from the pigment in the resin, not from a second shot. Multi-shot became the norm for later keyboards and for grip surfaces.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: two moulds in register on a rotating table, or a two-cavity shuttle

facts.label: Used for
facts.value: rubber feet, grip pads, hard/soft combinations

children.note: I could not confirm any two-colour feature on the 1982 breadbin case; this node records the technology that existed at the time and its realistic later use, and flags that the specific case is single-colour.

children.name: Two-colour / two-material injection machine
children.description: A press with two injection units and a rotating or shuttle plate so the second shot is made into the already-moulded first shot. The tooling must be indexable so the transfer happens while the part is still hot, which is why multi-shot tools are very expensive and hard to maintain.

children.name: Other polymers inside the case
children.description: The ABS case shares the machine with several other plastics. This node groups the second- and third-generation polymers in the C64's plastic parts so their feedstocks are traceable too.
children.note: Some of these plastics belong more naturally to the PCB, connector or PSU subsystems; they are listed here so the case-side plastic inventory is complete, with a note where the detail is owned elsewhere.

children.name: Polystyrene (GPPS / HIPS foam, trays)
children.description: General-purpose and impact polystyrene appear in the C64's plastic inventory as packaging foam and tray material rather than in the case itself. The case is ABS, not polystyrene - a common misconception.
children.note: GPPS and HIPS both come from styrene; see c64.case.abs-resin.styrene for the styrene supply chain, which is shared.

children.name: HIPS (impact-modified styrene)
children.description: Styrene polymerised in the presence of a polybutadiene graft rubber, exactly the same chemistry as ABS but with styrene replacing acrylonitrile. Made by bulk or emulsion polymerisation.
children.note: HIPS is chemically the same graft architecture as ABS, one substitution away; it is what you get when you drop the acrylonitrile. It is used for the foam end-caps and trays in the packaging.

children.name: Polycarbonate
children.description: Bisphenol A polycarbonate appears in clear covers, lens and shroud parts and in some clear case variants. It is made from bisphenol A and phosgene, and from the same BPA that comes out of cumene/benzene oxidation.
children.note: Polycarbonate is much more moisture- and temperature-sensitive than ABS; any clear C64 case is noticeably more prone to stress cracking than the opaque beige originals. Full supply chain sits under the plastics subsystem.

children.name: Cumene (for bisphenol A)
children.description: Propylene benzene alkylation product, separated from the C9 aromatics by distillation, then oxidised to cumene hydroperoxide and cleaved to phenol and acetone. Phenol + acetone -> bisphenol A -> phosgene + BPA -> polycarbonate.

facts.label: Formation
facts.value: benzene + propylene over phosphoric acid / zeolite

facts.label: Oxidation
facts.value: ~130 C, then acid cleavage to phenol + acetone

children.name: Polyoxymethylene (acetal / POM)
children.description: Acetal homopolymer and copolymer appear in precision mechanical parts - key plungers, small gears, latches - because POM is stiff, self-lubricating and dimensionally stable. It is made by polymerising formaldehyde from purified methanol.

facts.label: Key property
facts.value: low friction, high stiffness, good dimensional stability

children.note: Whether the C64 keyboard plungers are POM or a filled nylon is something I could not confirm; both were used for such parts in the period and both are moulded on the same 4-cavity key-plunger tools.

children.name: Methanol (from synthesis gas)
children.description: Made by reacting carbon monoxide and hydrogen from natural-gas reforming, a few hundred C and 50-100 bar over a copper/zinc oxide catalyst. Formaldehyde comes from methanol oxidation over silver or iron-molybdenum catalyst.

children.name: Nylon 6 / 6 (connector latches, clips)
children.description: Nylon is the classic connector and latch material: tough, slightly elastic, and it takes a good insert or press-fit without cracking. It appears in the latch tabs and clips that hold connectors in the case.

facts.label: Water absorption
facts.value: ~8% for 6,6 - it changes dimension with humidity

children.note: Nylon's high moisture uptake is why latches made of it can go slack over decades; a real reliability issue in 1980s consumer latches.

children.name: Adipic acid and hexamethylenediamine
children.description: Both are made from benzene or cyclohexane in the chemical chain: adipic acid by nitric oxidation of KA oil (cyclohexanol/cyclohexanone), and HMDA from butadiene via the NBS route (chlorination, ammonolysis, hydrogenation). Nylon 6,6 salt is then condensed.

children.name: PVC (cable jackets, sleeving)
children.description: The wire jackets, cable boots and some insulators in a C64 are PVC. PVC is made by polymerising vinyl chloride, and vinyl chloride comes from the chlor-ethylene route (EDC cracking to VCM plus HCl) or from oxychlorination of ethylene. The ethylene and the chlorine both come out of the same crackers and chlor-alkali plants that feed everything else.
children.note: The cable detail of this chain is expanded under c64.cables; this node exists so the case-side polymer inventory is complete.

children.name: Vinyl chloride monomer
children.description: Made by cracking EDC to VCM and HCl, then recombining HCl with ethylene (oxychlorination) or recovering HCl from the cracker. Then polymerised in a suspension autoclave - the classic 20-50 bar autoclave with a suspension agent - to PVC.

facts.label: EDC cracking
facts.value: ~500 C, 15-30 bar, packed or fluidised bed

children.name: Polyester / PET film (insulation, overlay)
children.description: Polyester film is used as thin insulation, as overlay film on some keycap legends, and as the amber capacitor sleeve material in the power supply. It comes from terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol, both of which come out of the aromatics and olefin chains already used elsewhere in the machine.
children.note: PET film and the keycap-overlay question overlap with the PCB and packaging detail; see c64.decor for the overlay decoration process and the board subsystem for the PCB materials.

children.name: Terephthalic acid (for PET film)
children.description: Made by air oxidation of para-xylene over cobalt-manganese acetate at 150-250 C and 10-40 bar, in a process that is a classic example of good process engineering: the oxidation is exothermic and the acetic acid byproduct is recycled.
children.note: The para-xylene comes from the same C8 aromatics separation that supplies o-xylene for the phthalic anhydride in the pigment, which is a nice convergence: one unit, two products.

children.name: Natural rubber (feet, grommets)
children.description: Some C64 feet and small grommets are natural rubber, cis-1,4-polyisoprene, made by coagulating latex tapped from Hevea brasiliensis. Natural rubber has excellent resilience and grip and ages to a tacky amber.

facts.label: Source
facts.value: latex from Hevea brasiliensis plantations, coagulated with acetic acid

children.note: The C64's four feet are more likely SBR or soft PVC than natural rubber; natural rubber is included because grommets and small vibration parts on Commodore equipment of this era were commonly natural rubber.

children.name: Natural rubber latex
children.description: Tapped from the rubber tree; the latex is preserved with ammonia, coagulated with acid, and the coagulum is pressed into sheets and smoke-cured. The tree is a plantation crop - rubber trees only yield for about 25 years and need a tropical climate.

children.name: Neoprene (chloroprene rubber)
children.description: Polychloroprene is used where oil and weather resistance matter - cable jackets on some Commodore leads, feet, and gasket material. It comes from chloroprene, made by chlorination of butadiene from the same C4 cracker cut.
children.note: Chloroprene is made by chlorinating butadiene from the cracker, so neoprene is another step downstream of the same C4 cut as the ABS rubber phase.

children.name: Epoxy (potting, die attach)
children.description: Epoxy resin is not a case material but appears as a potting and die-attach compound inside the machine - gluing the heat sink to the regulators and, in places, encapsulating a noisy analogue section. Epoxy comes from bisphenol A and epichlorohydrin, both aromatic-derived.

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: amine or anhydride, room temp to 120 C

children.note: Epoxy potting of the PSU and die attach is really part of the power and assembly subsystems; it is listed here for completeness because the C64's plastic inventory is often described as 'ABS only' and that is not quite right.

roots.name: Keyboard module: 66 keycaps on hybrid switches
roots.description: The C64's keyboard is a separate wired module that drops into the bezel: a steel backplate, a single-sided PCB carrying the matrix, 66 individually moulded ABS keycaps, and beneath each cap a Mitsumi-style hybrid switch - a moulded plunger with a conductive rubber pad and a metal return spring, closing a printed-circuit board contact when pressed. Legendas are printed onto the cap tops with a two-colour pad printer.

facts.label: Keys
facts.value: 66 total: 2 cursor-control keys, 4 function keys, 2 SHIFT, plus the alphanumerics and named keys

facts.label: Off-matrix keys
facts.value: RESTORE (dedicated NMI line) and SHIFT LOCK (shares the left-shift lines)

facts.label: Keyboard connector
facts.value: 24-pin header at CN1 on the mainboard, front-left edge

roots.note: The service manual states 'KEYS 66 Keys total'. The 8x8 matrix covers 64 positions; RESTORE bypasses the matrix entirely (it drives the non-maskable interrupt) and SHIFT LOCK is a latching key wired to the same lines as the left SHIFT, so to the machine it is indistinguishable from pressing left SHIFT.

children.name: Keycaps (66 individual moulded ABS caps)
children.description: Not a single dished sheet: 66 separate rectangular caps, each moulded in dark brown-grey ABS with a slightly concave top, each dropping through its own square opening in the bezel onto its own plunger. Some breadbin sets had tan-coloured function keys, others grey.

facts.label: Fitting
facts.value: cross-point: ~5 mm on early breadbin caps, ~3 mm on later ones

facts.label: Legend
facts.value: printed on the top face; later sets also on the front face

facts.label: Colour variation
facts.value: function keys tan on some sets, grey on others

children.note: The cross-point fitting and its shortening from ~5 mm to ~3 mm is a well-documented difference between early and late breadbin keyboards; caps from the two eras are not interchangeable. Legends on early sets are 1-3 mm down from the top of the cap; some sets use a bolder, some a thinner, font.

children.name: ABS grade for keycaps
children.description: A housing-grade ABS, low rubber content so the moulded texture stays crisp and the cap does not feel gummy. Keycap ABS is usually a slightly higher-gloss, higher-flow grade than the case resin because the caps are thin and have to fill a short, tight flow path.

facts.label: Wall thickness
facts.value: ~1.5-2 mm, thinnest in the legend area

children.note: The full ABS supply chain (cracker -> styrene/propylene/butadiene -> acrylonitrile -> emulsion graft -> compounding) is documented once under c64.case.abs-resin, because it is the same resin.

children.name: Flow and fill of a thin keycap
children.description: A keycap is one of the shortest flows in moulding: a shallow, thin-walled box filled through a single gate. It is a classic short-shot candidate, which is why keycap tools are small multi-cavity tools with a well-placed gate and a warm mould so the flow front does not freeze before the last corner fills.

facts.label: Gate
facts.value: single, on the inside wall away from the legend face

children.name: Keycap tool (small multi-cavity, hardened steel)
children.description: Keycaps are made in small high-cavity tools - 4, 8 or 16 cavities in one block - because a cap is cheap and the tool has to be small enough to fit a small press. The tool is hardened tool steel, and the caps come off a common gate so the visible faces are identical.

facts.label: Tool life
facts.value: 300,000-1,000,000 shots; replated and repolished on rebuild

children.note: This is the same tool steel and the same polish-and-plate route as the case tool; the difference is size and cavity count, not materials.

children.name: Printed keycap legends
children.description: Legends are printed on the cap top with a two-colour pad printer (pad printing / tampo printing): a soft silicone pad picks up ink from a cliche, deforms against the slightly crowned cap, and transfers the character. White legends on the dark caps; the RETURN and SHIFT caps in some sets get legends on the front face too.

facts.label: Why pad and not screen
facts.value: a flat cap top with a slight crown will not lie flat under a screen; pad printing conforms

facts.label: Legends
facts.value: single character on most keys; shifted and graphic characters on the front face of later sets

children.note: The ink chemistry and the pad/cliche supply chain are detailed under c64.decor. Later Commodore sets printed the whole character set on the top face only, with RETURN and SHIFT labels offset to a corner.

children.name: Front-face legends (shifted / graphic characters)
children.description: On sets that carry the shifted and graphic characters, these are printed on the small front wall of the cap. Printing a vertical face with a pad printer needs the pad tilted and a second fixture, which is why early sets avoided it and used a bolder single top legend.

facts.label: Fixture
facts.value: cap held tilted in a nest

facts.label: Coverage
facts.value: improves gradually across the production run

children.note: The extent to which a given run printed front legends varies; the breadbox64 write-up notes the front-side printing on later C64C sets and thinner fonts on some breadbin sets.

children.name: Keycap colours and any colour coding
children.description: Breadbin C64 caps are almost uniformly a dark brown-grey, with function keys sometimes a lighter grey or tan. There is no per-number colour coding on the breadbin keyboard - that idea belongs to some other machines (the C64C and later Commodore sets vary, and the VIC-20 had differently coloured function keys). What a C64 keycap has is a moulded-in colour, not a printed colour.

facts.label: Number-key coding
facts.value: none on the breadbin; legends are all one colour on the cap

children.note: I could not confirm any colour-coded number row or overlay on the 1982 breadbin keyboard. Where a legend colour differs between sets it tracks the cap colour, not the key function. Treat any claim of printed colour-coded number overlays as unverified for this machine.

children.name: Cross-point fitting and cap underside
children.description: The underside of the cap carries a moulded cross that clips onto the matching cross-post on the plunger - about 5 mm on early breadbin caps, about 3 mm on later ones. The two are not interchangeable. The underside also has guide ribs that keep the cap square as it travels.

facts.label: Material
facts.value: moulded with the cap, same ABS

children.name: Hybrid switches (Mitsumi-style plunger, rubber dome, spring)
children.description: The C64 does not use a rubber-dome-only membrane like a calculator, nor a mechanical switch like a typewriter. It uses a hybrid: a moulded plunger carrying a conductive rubber pad rides on a coil spring, and pressing it drives a gold or carbon contact onto a PCB pad. That gives a real click, a light touch and a definite bottom-out - which is why a C64 keyboard still feels 'mechanical' in the 1980s sense.

facts.label: Force
facts.value: roughly 55-70 gf at the snap peak for a typical hybrid plunger

facts.label: Life
facts.value: 10-30 million operations rated for these switches

children.note: Retroleum's keyboard notes describe 'Type 1' keyboards with black plungers, springs under all keys, and ~5 mm cross-points, versus 'Type 2' with white four-pronged plungers, grey rubber bubble contacts and a metal spring only under the space bar.

children.name: Switch plunger (moulded, with conductive rubber)
children.description: A small moulded body with a cross-post on top that the keycap clips onto, one or more arms that carry a conductive rubber pad, and a stem that slides in the keyboard body. Type 2 plungers have four prongs and carry a loose grey 'bubble' contact.

facts.label: Type 1
facts.value: black plungers, springs under every key, metal contact

facts.label: Type 2
facts.value: white four-pronged plungers, grey rubber bubble contacts, spring under the space bar only

children.name: Plunger polymer (acetal / filled nylon)
children.description: The plunger has to be dimensionally stable over millions of strokes and low-friction against the spring and the body. Acetal (POM) is the classic choice for its low friction and stiffness; glass-filled nylon or polycarbonate are also used. All three are moulded on small multi-cavity tools.

facts.label: Friction
facts.value: POM has a very low coefficient of friction and no 'grease needed' behaviour

children.note: Which polymer each production run used is not something I could pin down; POM and filled nylon were both routine. The formaldehyde and nylon chains are documented under c64.case.other-polymers.

children.name: Conductive rubber contact (carbon-loaded silicone)
children.description: The contact is a small pad of silicone rubber loaded with conductive carbon black. The carbon particles touch each other and carry a small current across the PCB pad when the pad is pressed down, closing the switch. It needs to be conductive enough to bridge the gold contact but resistive enough not to be a dead short.

facts.label: Matrix
facts.value: silicone rubber (VMQ), cured with a peroxide

children.name: Silicone rubber (the matrix of the conductive pad)
children.description: Polydimethylsiloxane. The base polymer is made by ring-opening polymerisation of octamethylcyclotetrasiloxane or by equilibration of a silanol-terminated PDMS; fillers (silica, silicone oil) tune the hardness and the tear strength.

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: peroxide (e.g. dicumyl peroxide) or addition-cure platinum

facts.label: Shore hardness
facts.value: Shore A 40-70 for a contact pad

children.name: Fumed / precipitated silica filler
children.description: Reinforcing silica for the silicone rubber. It is made either by fuming silicon tetrachloride in a flame or by precipitating from a sodium silicate solution. Both routes end at quartz sand or silicon metal.

facts.label: Fumed route
facts.value: SiCl4 + H2 + O2 -> SiO2 + HCl at ~1000-1400 C flame

facts.label: Precipitated route
facts.value: water glass acidification, from quartz sand + soda ash

children.name: Silicon metal (from quartz)
children.description: Quartz sand (SiO2) is reduced with carbon in a submerged-arc furnace at about 2000 C to give 98-99% silicon. This is the starting point for the whole silicon chemistry, and here it ends up in a rubber pad rather than in a chip.

children.name: Carbon black filler
children.description: The conductive filler. Furnace black is made by feeding oil or gas to a hot refractory-carbon reactor in a stream of air at 1200-1500 C, quenching the soot, then pelletising and grinding it. It is the same carbon black family used in tyre rubber.

facts.label: Feed
facts.value: heavy oil / aromatic residue from petroleum refining

children.note: A striking example of convergence: the tyre in a car and the switch contact in a C64 keyboard are loaded with essentially the same furnace black, from the same heavy-oil feed.

children.name: Compounding the conductive silicone pad
children.description: Silicone rubber, conductive carbon black, a peroxide cure and a filler are mixed on a two-roll mill, then the pad is either transfer-moulded or printed as a dot on the plunger. Getting the carbon black well dispersed without overworking it is the whole trick: too little mixing leaves lumps that do not conduct, too much breaks down the carbon network and the pad stops conducting.

facts.label: Mixing
facts.value: two-roll mill or internal mixer, 60-120 C

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: peroxide or addition-cure; press or transfer mould

facts.label: Cure time/temperature
facts.value: e.g. 10 min at 150 C, or seconds in a fast cure

children.name: Two-roll compounding mill
children.description: Two counter-rotating chilled rolls nip the compound and disperse the filler. It is the oldest and still the most reliable way to get a clean dispersion, and every rubber and plasticiser maker owns one.

facts.label: Roll gap
facts.value: adjustable, often with a gauge for final nip

children.name: Cure system (peroxide crosslinker)
children.description: Silicone rubber needs a crosslinker. Dicumyl peroxide is the classic general-purpose choice for a compression-moulded pad; addition-cure (platinum-catalysed) systems came later and cure faster with less shrink.

children.name: Dicumyl peroxide
children.description: The commonest silicone crosslinker of the era. It is made from cumene: cumene is oxidised to cumene hydroperoxide and then condensed with alpha-methylstyrene to give dicumyl peroxide.

facts.label: Decomposition
facts.value: gives a free radical at ~120-160 C, driving silicone crosslinking

children.name: Alpha-methylstyrene
children.description: A C9 vinylbenzene used as a chain-transfer agent and as the co-reactant in dicumyl peroxide. It is made by dehydrating cumene over alumina or acid at ~300-400 C - a direct route from the same C9 aromatics that make cumene itself.

children.name: Cumene to hydroperoxide and alpha-methylstyrene
children.description: Cumene is air-oxidised in a stirred liquid-phase reactor at ~100-140 C to cumene hydroperoxide. Part is condensed with alpha-methylstyrene to make dicumyl peroxide; part is acid-cleaved to phenol and acetone, which goes on to bisphenol A and epoxy. One plant, three products.

facts.label: Oxidation
facts.value: ~100-140 C, 4-10 bar, air bubbled through cumene

children.note: This is a textbook example of how a single 1970s-era petrochemical plant feeds the whole plastics complex: phenol to epoxy and polycarbonate, cumene to rubber and peroxides.

children.name: Cumene from benzene and propylene
children.description: Propylene is alkylated onto benzene over phosphoric acid on silica (or a zeolite) at 300-450 C and 20-60 bar to give cumene, which is separated from its polyalkylated heavies by distillation.

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: phosphoric acid on silica, or a zeolite

children.name: Return spring (music wire)
children.description: A small coil spring under each key that returns the plunger. It is drawn from music wire (a high-carbon, low-carbon-content steel with a tight tensile range) and wound on a automatic spring coiler. Type 1 keyboards spring every key; Type 2 springs only the space bar and relies on the rubber dome elsewhere.

facts.label: Rate
facts.value: set so the snap peak lands at 55-70 gf

children.name: Music wire (patented steel)
children.description: A high-carbon, low-carbon-content alloy steel with very tight mechanical properties and a very clean surface - patented in the 1880s for piano wire. It is drawn to fine gauge on a bull-block or continuous wire drawer and patented through a multi-step process.

facts.label: Carbon
facts.value: ~0.8-0.9% (music wire is high carbon, spring wire lower)

facts.label: Process
facts.value: patenting: quench, patenting heat, over-drawing in dies

children.name: The snap: force-displacement curve of the switch
children.description: The 'feel' of a C64 key is a curve, not a number. The plunger rides down the spring, then the rubber dome on the PCB has to collapse (or the contact arm has to snap over), producing a peak in force; past the peak the force drops as the dome collapses, then rises again into the bottom-out. Peak-to-valley difference of maybe 20-30 gf is what the finger reads as 'clicky'.
children.note: These are typical figures for hybrid plunger/dome switches of this period, not measured C64 data. C64 keys are famous for a light, crisp action; the rubber dome's collapse is what gives the characteristic feel.

children.name: Keyboard PCB (matrix and contacts)
children.description: A single-sided PCB carrying the 8x8 matrix traces and one contact pad per switch, sitting under the plungers. The keyboard PCB plugs into a 24-pin header on the mainboard (CN1) and carries no logic of its own - it is just a switch matrix that the CIA scans.
children.note: The board material and the copper/gold plating processes belong to the PCB subsystem; this node exists so the keyboard's own parts are complete.

children.name: Matrix topology and the two odd keys
children.description: The CIA drives one of eight rows low and reads the eight columns; a pressed key connects one row to one column. Sixty-four positions are scanned. RESTORE is wired straight to the NMI line, bypassing the matrix, which is why RESTORE works even while the CPU is jammed.
