SHIFT LOCK is a mechanically latching switch wired to the same two lines as the left SHIFT.

facts.label: RESTORE
facts.value: dedicated line to NMI, not scanned

facts.label: SHIFT LOCK
facts.value: latching; shares the left-shift matrix lines

children.note: SHIFT LOCK being on the same lines as left SHIFT is why holding shift lock in software is impossible and why BASIC sees a shift, not a separate key.

children.name: Contact pads (gold or carbon)
children.description: Each switch lands on a printed pad. On gold-plated keyboards the pad is gold over nickel; on cheaper sets it is a carbon/graphite coating on the copper. The contact on the plunger is the conductive rubber; the pad is the fixed electrode.
children.note: Retroleum notes the contacts on the PCB are either gold or carbon plated and that the most common keyboard fault is dust on the backplate PCB or dirt on the plunger's conductive pads - cleaned with isopropyl alcohol.

children.name: Steel backplate
children.description: A sheet-steel plate under the PCB with punched openings for the plungers and rolled or pressed stiffening beads. It carries the springs and holds the plungers' travel, and it is screwed to the keyboard body with about twenty small gold-coloured screws.

children.name: Piercing and forming of the backplate
children.description: The openings are pierced on a punch press in a single stroke across the whole sheet; the stiffening beads are then roll-formed. This is a high-volume sheet-metal process: a tonne of steel punched this way costs a fraction of a machined equivalent.
children.note: Cold-rolled mild steel sheet is made by hot rolling a slab and then cold rolling it; the cold rolling is what gives the smooth surface and the accurate punches.

children.name: Keyboard body and its fasteners
children.description: A moulded ABS body that holds the plungers, the PCB and the backplate, and carries the cable. It is retained by about twenty small gold-coloured screws, and on the shift-lock position it has a black-backed keyswitch with one wire running diagonally to the PCB.

facts.label: Shift lock
facts.value: black-backed keyswitch, one wire runs diagonally to the PCB

children.note: Retroleum's teardown notes that the SHIFT LOCK keyswitch is a black-backed switch with one wire soldered diagonally across the board - a small manufacturing quirk that tells you the module was hand-assembled.

children.name: Shift-lock keyswitch
children.description: A tiny mechanically-latching slide switch (a black plastic body with a metal leaf contact) that holds itself in the shifted position until pressed again. It is not a matrix key at all - it is a separate latch that closes the shift lines.

children.name: Keyboard retaining screws (gold-coloured)
children.description: Roughly twenty small self-tapping screws with a gold or brass finish hold the keyboard backplate and body together. The gold colour is a zinc-nickel or brass-look plating, chosen because it reads as 'quality' on a part the customer never sees.

children.name: Keyboard ribbon cable and connector
children.description: A short flat ribbon or discrete-lead cable from the keyboard to the 24-pin header (CN1) on the front-left edge of the mainboard, terminating in a moulded connector housing. It carries the eight matrix rows, the eight columns, the RESTORE line and the power rails - twenty-four conductors.

children.name: Ribbon conductors
children.description: Either a laminated flat-flex ribbon (etched copper on polyimide film) or discrete stranded wires. Ribbon is thinner; discrete leads are more flexible at the fold and are what most Commodore keyboard cables used.
children.note: Whether a given C64 keyboard cable is flat-flex or discrete is a per-run detail; both are consistent with the era and with the 24-pin connector.

roots.name: Supplied cables: RF lead, A/V lead, mains cord
roots.description: Three cables shipped with or sold alongside a breadbin C64. The RF cable carries the modulator's VHF output from the machine's phono socket to a television's aerial input, so it is a 75-ohm coaxial. The A/V lead carries luma, chroma, composite and audio to a monitor through an 8-pin DIN. The mains cord is a two- or three-core PVC-jacketed cord with a moulded plug that feeds the external power supply.

facts.label: A/V socket
facts.value: 8-pin DIN, CN5 on the motherboard, on early sets a 5-pin socket

facts.label: Switch box
facts.value: Commodore part 904778-01, an RF splitter/box accessory

roots.note: The breadbin's RF modulator sits on the motherboard (Astec or Mitsumi depending on production run) and its output leaves through the machine's own phono socket. The supplied RF cable is therefore a coax lead with a phono plug at the C64 end and a television-plug at the TV end. Early boards used a 5-pin video socket; later ones an 8-pin DIN, which changes the A/V cable but not the RF cable.

children.name: RF cable (phono plug to TV plug)
children.description: A 75-ohm coaxial lead. Its job is to get a 1 MHz video signal, sitting on a VHF carrier, into a television's analogue aerial input without picking up half the room on the way. Impedance matching and a decent screen are what keep the picture from ghosting.

facts.label: TV end
facts.value: coaxial television plug (the old round type)

children.name: 75-ohm coaxial cable
children.description: Centre conductor, dielectric, braid screen, PVC jacket. The braid is what does the shielding; the jacket is only there to survive being dragged under a TV cabinet for twenty years.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: solid or stranded centre conductor, PE or PTFE dielectric, braided tinned-copper screen, PVC jacket

children.note: A consumer RF lead of this type was often a thin-wall 75-ohm coax rather than a strict RG designation; the important properties are 75 ohm and a full-coverage screen.

children.name: Centre conductor (copper, or copper-clad steel)
children.description: The signal-carrying core. Consumer coax uses solid bare copper or, to save money, copper-clad steel. At RF frequencies a CCS core is perfectly adequate for a metre of cable.

children.name: Copper wire rod and drawing
children.description: Copper cathodes are melted, cast into wire rod, then drawn through a series of dies to the finished diameter. A cable plant buys rod and draws it in-house; drawing anneals and work-hardens the copper in the same step.

facts.label: Drawing
facts.value: wet or dry, through carbide or diamond dies

children.note: The copper supply chain (chalcopyrite ore -> flotation -> flash smelting -> converting -> tankhouse electrolysis) is documented once under c64.case.abs-resin.chalcopyrite; the same cathode feeds every copper conductor in the machine.

children.name: Dielectric (polyethylene or PTFE)
children.description: The insulating foam between conductor and braid. Polyethylene is the volume material for consumer coax, often gas-injected or foam-injected to lower the dielectric constant and hold 75 ohm with a bigger centre conductor. PTFE (Teflon) is the low-loss, low-noise alternative used where a very clean signal or a tight bend radius matters.

facts.label: Premium choice
facts.value: PTFE for low loss and low dielectric constant

facts.label: Extrusion
facts.value: pre-extruded dielectric tube, then conductor drawn in

children.note: Foamed polyethylene is worth noting because it is the same polymer as the plastic bags in the packaging: chain-grafted or chemical-blowing-agent foam, blown in the extrusion line.

children.name: Cable extrusion line
children.description: A vertical or horizontal line where conductor is drawn through a die, dielectric tube is extruded or foamed around it, braid is laid on from a rotating carrier, and the jacket is extruded and cooled in a trough. Cable extrusion is one of the few polymer processes that is genuinely continuous and high-speed.

facts.label: Steps
facts.value: conductor -> dielectric -> braid -> jacket, often on separate lines

facts.label: Spark testing
facts.value: each length passes a high-voltage spark tester

children.name: Braided screen (tinned copper)
children.description: A flat bundle of tinned copper wires woven over the dielectric by a braiding machine, usually with a second pass to push coverage from ~70% toward 90%. Tinning reduces oxidation and makes the braid easier to terminate.
children.note: Coverage is the number that matters: a 70%-covered braid leaks RF, and that leakage is why a badly-made RF cable puts a visible ghost on the picture.

children.name: Low-density polyethylene (the volume dielectric)
children.description: The bulk of consumer coax dielectric is LDPE made by high-pressure or low-pressure polymerisation of ethylene. LDPE is branched and low-density, which is exactly what you want here: the branching lowers the dielectric constant so the coaxial geometry lands on 75 ohm with a reasonable centre-conductor size.

children.name: LDPE polymerisation of ethylene
children.description: Ethylene is polymerised either at high pressure (1000-3000 bar, 200-300 C, initiated by peroxides) or at low pressure with a Ziegler-Natta catalyst (20-40 bar, 70-110 C). Cable plants typically run high-pressure LDPE because it extrudes cleanly and fast; low-pressure LLDPE is the modern preference for some uses.
children.note: High-pressure LDPE is still made the same way today; the difference between 1982 and now is mainly catalyst control and polymer-grade consistency, not the process.

children.name: Ziegler-Natta catalyst (TiCl4 + alkylaluminium)
children.description: The low-pressure catalyst: titanium tetrachloride supported on magnesium chloride with an aluminium alkyl co-catalyst. It polymerises ethylene in a stereoregular way and gives the higher-density grades.

children.name: Titanium tetrachloride
children.description: Made by chlorinating titanium metal or a titanium-bearing slag at 400-900 C in carbon or fluidised bed. The metal itself is made by the Kroll process: rutile or ilmenite is chlorinated to TiCl4, which is reduced with magnesium metal.

facts.label: Chlorination
facts.value: 400-900 C, with coke or in a fluidised bed

facts.label: Kroll reduction
facts.value: TiCl4 + 2 Mg -> Ti + 2 MgCl2, 800-900 C under argon

children.name: Rutile / ilmenite feedstock for titanium metal
children.description: The same titanium ores that make the white pigment in the case, here reduced to sponge titanium and then chlorinated for the polymerisation catalyst. One ore, two very different products.

children.name: Aluminium alkyl co-catalyst
children.description: Aluminium triethyl or aluminium diethyl, made by reacting aluminium with the corresponding alkyl chloride. It is what activates the titanium and controls the polymer's branching.
children.note: Ethyl chloride comes from hydrochlorination of ethylene, so this catalyst reaches back into the same ethylene/chlorine pool as the PVC.

children.name: Polymerisation-grade ethylene purity
children.description: Cable-grade polyethylene needs a very clean monomer: oxygen, water, sulphur and acetylene all poison or degrade the polymer. Ethylene from the cracker is therefore purified to 99.9%+ by distillation, molecular sieves and catalyst scrubbing before it reaches a reactor.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 99.9%+, with O2 and H2O at ppb

facts.label: Purification
facts.value: multi-column distillation, molecular sieve drying, guard beds

children.note: This is a good example of why the same chemical sold as 'ethylene' has a ladder of grades, and why the price of a cable-grade polymer is set by the polymer, not by the monomer.

children.name: Outer jacket (PVC)
children.description: A lead-compounded PVC jacket, usually flexible grade with a plasticiser so the cable stays bendable. The jacket has nothing to do with the signal; its job is abrasion and handling.

children.name: Plasticiser in flexible PVC
children.description: Cable PVC is not rigid: it is compounded with a plasticiser such as dioctyl phthalate (DOP) or trimellitates, dropped into an extruder at 5-10% and mixed before extrusion. The plasticiser is what makes the lead supple instead of stiff and brittle.
children.note: DOP is made from phthalic anhydride (via phthalate esterification with 2-ethylhexanol), and the 2-ethylhexanol comes from hydroformylation of propylene - so a cable jacket shares its whole feedstock chain with the pigment in the case.

children.name: Moulded phono plug and TV plug
children.description: Both ends are moulded: a phono (RCA) plug with a nickel-plated centre pin in a moulded barrel at the C64 end, and a television coaxial plug at the other. The pin is plated rather than bare so it survives being shoved in and out of the TV a thousand times.

facts.label: Barrel
facts.value: knurled, presses onto or screws onto the cable jacket

children.name: Nickel plating of the pin
children.description: Electrolytic nickel plating on a brass pin, giving a hard, corrosion-resistant, non-tarnishing surface. Nickel is the classic choice for connector contacts because its contact resistance stays low and it does not corrode in a socket.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: sulfate or sulfamate nickel, with a brightening additive

children.note: Nickel comes as ferronickel (from laterite ore or from matte), not as a pure metal. It is one of the few metals whose demand in the 1980s was genuinely driven by consumer plating rather than by steel.

children.name: Brass pin stock
children.description: Free-cutting brass (typically leaded brass) machined or cold-formed into the pin and barrel. Brass is the standard connector material because it machines well, springs enough to take a wipe, and does not rust.

children.name: Strain-relief boot
children.description: A moulded rubber or PVC boot at each cable end where it enters the plug body, taking the bending load so the conductor does not fatigue at the termination. Cheap to add, and the difference between a lead that survives ten years and one that breaks at the root.

facts.label: Form
facts.value: moulded-in taper or a slid-on sleeve

children.name: Cable assembly and test
children.description: Cables are made by cutting, stripping, crimping or soldering the conductor into the plug, moulding or snapping the plug body on, and testing. A continuity and insulation-resistance check, often on an automatic line tester, catches the faults before the lead reaches the box.

facts.label: Tests
facts.value: continuity, insulation resistance, and for coax a capacitance or impedance check

facts.label: Typical labour
facts.value: a minute or two per lead on a semi-automatic line

children.note: Cable assembly is one of the lowest-marginal-cost steps in consumer electronics, which is why Commodore and its contract manufacturers made leads in enormous volume in Hong Kong and Taiwan.

children.name: A/V cable to a 1701/1702 monitor
children.description: A monitor lead carrying luma, chroma, composite video, audio in and out, and +5V/ground, in an 8-pin DIN connector at each end. It was often bundled with the monitor rather than sold with the computer, which is why many C64 owners improvised with a phono lead for composite only.

facts.label: Connector
facts.value: 8-pin DIN (CN5); early machines used a 5-pin socket

facts.label: Signals
facts.value: luma, chroma, composite, audio out, audio in, +5 V, ground

children.name: DIN connector and cable
children.description: A moulded DIN plug with a metal shell and a screw-on or clip-on backshell that clamps the cable and provides strain relief. The shell is nickel-plated steel or brass, and the interior is filled with a phenolic or thermoplastic insert holding the female contacts.

facts.label: Insert
facts.value: phenolic or thermoplastic, holding the contacts

children.note: The DIN plug is a European standard (DIN 41512) and is one of the few connectors where the C64's whole monitor ecosystem was deliberately European.

children.name: Cable conductors and insulation
children.description: Stranded tinned copper conductors with PVC insulation, colour-coded to the DIN pinout. Shielded or twisted pairs for the audio lines to keep the 1 MHz clock out of the speaker.

children.name: Mains power cord
children.description: A detachable mains lead for the external power supply: two or three PVC-insulated copper conductors in a moulded outer jacket, with a moulded mains plug at one end and a moulded figure-8 or IEC connector at the other. In Europe it is a two-pin contour plug; in North America a three-pin NEMA plug, often polarised.

facts.label: Insulation
facts.value: PVC per conductor; outer jacket PVC or rubber

facts.label: Current
facts.value: 2.5 A or 10 A rated, well over the C64's ~15 W draw

facts.label: Connector
facts.value: figure-8 (C7) or IEC C8 inlet on the power supply

children.name: Stranded copper conductors
children.description: Fine-strand flexible copper, made by bunching many small wires in a roving machine and twisting them. Flexible stranding is what lets a mains lead bend without breaking the strands.

children.name: PVC insulation extruded onto the conductors
children.description: Each conductor is passed through a die in an extrusion line and coated with a rigid or semi-rigid PVC at a few hundred volts' worth of insulation. Extrusion is continuous and the colour is added by pigment masterbatch.

children.name: Outer jacket
children.description: A second extrusion over the assembled, twisted conductors. The conductors are first twisted together on a planetary twister so the cord resists unwinding, then jacketed.

facts.label: Cord twist
facts.value: planetary or bunch twisting, tens of twists per metre

children.name: Moulded mains plug
children.description: A plug with a thermoplastic cord body wrapped around the cable entry to take the bending strain, and two or three brass prongs riveted or crimped in. The cord body is the part that actually fails: the plug is unbolted from the prongs and slides off the cable.

facts.label: Prongs
facts.value: brass, plated, on the North American 3-pin plug also nickel-plated

children.name: Brass prongs
children.description: Blanked, formed and plated brass strip. Brass is used rather than steel because it must not spark and must not corrode; the plating gives the dull, non-tarnishing surface a moulded plug has.

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: brass strip, often leaded free-cutting grade

children.name: Cord body / strain-relief grip
children.description: Moulded in PVC or polypropylene and over-moulded onto the jacket. It is deliberately flexible so the cable can swivel, which is also why a moulded cord body eventually tears at its root after years of being yanked out of a wall socket by the wire.

children.name: TV switch box (optional accessory)
children.description: Commodore part 904778-01, an external box that let the C64's RF output share a television aerial socket with an actual antenna, switching between them. It is an accessory rather than a cable, but it is in the same moulded-plastic-and-coax family and shares the cable supply chain.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: switch between computer RF and TV aerial

children.note: The service-manual parts list gives this number; its exact internals are not documented in the sources I found.

roots.name: Retail packaging: printed box, foam, polybag, manual
roots.description: A breadbin C64 shipped in a corrugated board box printed lithographically with Commodore's rainbow graphics, with the machine cradled in two moulded polystyrene end blocks and wrapped in a polyethylene bag, plus the user's manual and a warranty card. Boxes went to a corrugated master carton on a timber skid for shipping to warehouses.

facts.label: Box
facts.value: corrugated board, lithographically printed, rainbow graphics

facts.label: Bag
facts.value: plain polyethylene sleeve over the machine

facts.label: Paperwork
facts.value: user's manual (Commodore part 320974) and a warranty/registration card

roots.note: Internal packaging varied by region, by production run and by whether the machine was sold boxed or shipped in bulk to a distributor, so 'the C64 box' is really several packages: an early plain brown box with a rainbow stripe, later 'rainbow' graphics, and machined-in plain boxes. The user's manual is documented as Commodore part 320974 in the service-manual parts list. I could not verify the exact internal foam arrangement for every region.

children.name: Retail corrugated box
children.description: A regular slotted container or a tuck-end box in B-flute corrugated board, printed on a sheet-fed or web offset press in up to four or six colours plus a rainbow gradient, then creased, cut and glued. It is a commodity: the board is a mill product and the printing is a printshop product, not a Commodore product.

children.name: Corrugated board (liner + medium)
children.description: Two kraft liners glued to a fluted medium. In 1982 a consumer-electronics box was usually C-flute or B-flute single wall, made from semichemical or recycled kraft; the flute is what gives the box its edge crush strength for a couple of Newtons of stacking force.

facts.label: Structure
facts.value: liner / fluted medium / liner, single wall

facts.label: Adhesive
facts.value: starch or dextrin, hot-water resistant grade

children.name: Kraft liner (topside and underside)
children.description: Unbleached paper made from long-fibre softwood pulp, typically 120-200 gsm. Its brown colour is the kraft process itself: the pulp is brown before it reaches the paper machine, because the kraft cook keeps the lignin.

children.name: Kraft pulp
children.description: Wood chips are steamed, cooked in a kraft digester with sodium hydroxide and sodium sulfide, washed, and bleached only lightly. The brown colour is retained kraft lignin, which is why kraft paper is brown and recycling it is easy.

children.name: Wood chips from sawmill waste
children.description: Roundwood is debarked and chipped into 20-30 mm chips in a disc chipper, ready for the digester. The chips are the whole reason the paper mill sits next to a forest: you cannot make paper without wood fibre.

children.name: Roundwood logs
children.description: Trunk sections felled and delimbed, usually conifer in northern Europe and North America. Softwood is preferred for kraft because its long fibres give paper strength; hardwoods go into hardwood kraft or into mechanical pulp.

children.name: Planted softwood stand
children.description: Managed conifer plantations (spruce, pine, or southern pine) felled on a rotation and replanted. This is where the fibre chain ends: a box is wood, and the wood is a tree that was grown, cut and chipped.

children.name: Kraft cooking (digestion)
children.description: Chips are cooked in a spherical or continuous digester with white liquor (sodium hydroxide + sodium sulfide + sodium carbonate) at 160-180 C. The alkali dissolves the lignin; the sulfide keeps the dissolved lignin in solution so the fibres do not darken.

facts.label: Chemical recovery
facts.value: black liquor is evaporated and burnt to regenerate the chemicals

children.name: Caustic soda for the digester
children.description: The same chlor-alkali caustic that makes VCM and soaps comes to the paper mill, typically as a 50% solution in tank cars.

children.name: Brown (kraft) grade versus bleached
children.description: Unbleached kraft keeps its brown colour and is the cheapest strong liner. A bleached or semi-bleached top liner costs more and is used where the print needs a white background. Commodore's boxes are brown board with printing on top, so the brown liner is exactly right.

facts.label: Bleaching
facts.value: chlorine, chlorine dioxide or oxygen/peroxide delignification

children.note: Chlorine bleaching of pulp was standard in 1982 and has since been largely displaced by chlorine-free processes for environmental reasons - a clear 1980s-vs-modern difference in the same plant.

children.name: Fourdrinier paper machine
children.description: The pulp is diluted to a few tenths of a percent solids and laid as a continuous web on a moving wire mesh, squeezed, dried over felt-covered heated cylinders, calendered, and wound onto reels. This machine is where a tree becomes a sheet.

facts.label: Web speed
facts.value: 300-600 m/min on a modern machine; slower in 1982

children.name: Fluted medium (recycled)
children.description: The wavy centre of the board is usually made from 100% recycled paper, because the flute does not need virgin-fibre strength. Old corrugated boxes are collected, pulped (the recycled / OCF route), and run onto a corrugating machine.

children.name: Recovered paper (OCC / mixed waste)
children.description: Collected corrugated and box board, baled, repulped in a hydrapulper and screened. The deinking stage is needed for printed waste; unprinted OCC is repulped as it is. The fibre in a C64 box's fluted medium is therefore almost certainly several previous boxes.

facts.label: Grade
facts.value: OCC (old corrugated container) or mixed waste paper

children.name: Repulping and deinking
children.description: Bales are dropped into a hydrapulper, torn up into fibre, screened, and deinked with a flotation cell and surfactant to remove printing inks. A high proportion of the world's corrugated medium fibre is recovered in exactly this way.

children.name: Corrugating and sheet making
children.description: Medium paper is corrugated between two rotating fluted rolls with heat and starch glue, then glued to liners; the sheet is cut and creased. The board then goes to the box plant for slotting, folding and gluing.

facts.label: Fibre
facts.value: reuse office paper makes poor medium; box fibre is preferred

children.note: The reason a pizza box folds and a used sheet does not: the flute is a beam. C64 boxes are usually single-wall B or C flute.

children.name: Starch corrugating adhesive
children.description: The glue holding the flutes and the liners is a corn- or tapioca-starch dextrin, cooked on the corrugator and applied hot. It is the standard adhesive in corrugated board and the reason the board is not a fire hazard in the way solvent glues would be.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: starch / dextrin, hot-water resistant grade for the liners

children.name: Corn (maize) starch
children.description: Starch is wet-milled from maize: the kernels are steeped in warm water to soften the germ, ground, and the starch is separated by gravity or centrifugally and dried. Every corrugated box is glued with a plant, not a petrochemical.

children.name: Maize crop
children.description: A cereal grain grown in enormous tonnages in the US corn belt and in Europe, China and Brazil; the harvested cobs are shelled and the kernels go to wet milling. This is the agricultural end of the adhesive chain.

children.name: Box printing (offset litho) and the rainbow graphics
children.description: The printed sheet is run on an offset litho press - sheet-fed for short runs, web-fed for long runs - in a small number of process colours, with the Commodore rainbow reproduced as a multi-stop gradient. The board is then cut, creased and glued.

facts.label: Press
facts.value: sheet-fed offset or rotary web offset

facts.label: Colours
facts.value: typically 3-6 process colours; the rainbow needs extra separations or a duotone gradient

facts.label: Surface
facts.value: uncoated kraft board; often a thin aqueous varnish for scuff resistance

children.note: Flexographic printing on corrugate with rubber or photopolymer plates became the normal route for high-run corrugated print during this period and later; for a mid-run consumer box in the early 1980s, sheet-fed offset on a liner was still common.

children.name: Offset lithographic printing
children.description: The image is on a flat plate, wetted with dampening solution so the image areas reject ink, and printed by a rubber blanket onto paper. Litho gives fine detail and consistent colour on uncoated board, at the cost of a plate-making step per colour.

children.name: Lithographic printing plate
children.description: A thin aluminium or copper plate, grained and treated, with a photopolymer or metal-image layer carrying the separations. The classic long-run offset plate is an aluminium sheet electro-grained and anodised; short runs use photopolymer plates directly.

children.name: Offset printing ink
children.description: A pigment dispersed in a drying-oil-based vehicle (linseed/soy alkyd) with resin, wax and a drier. Water-based offset inks became the norm for corrugated in the 1990s; oil-based inks were standard in 1982.

facts.label: Pigments
facts.value: titanium dioxide white, phthalocyanine blues, phthalochromate yellows

children.name: Alkyd / drying-oil ink vehicle
children.description: Built from vegetable oil (linseed or soybean) fatty acids condensed with a polyol and a phthalic or maleic anhydride, then crosslinked by oxidative polymerisation on the press. So the ink vehicle on the box traces back to a phthalic anhydride plant, the same chemistry as the pigment in the case.

children.name: Soy or linseed oil (ink vehicle base)
children.description: A vegetable oil pressed from a crop. It oxidises (dries) on the printed sheet, which is what 'drying ink' means. In 1982 soybean oil was becoming the preferred ink vehicle because of the 1970s linseed-oil shortages.

children.name: Ink pigments (organic and inorganic)
children.description: In 1982 most packaging colourants were still inorganic: iron oxides, chrome yellow, ultramarine. The bright synthetic organic pigments (phthalocyanines, azo yellows) were used for the saturated rainbow, and the titanium dioxide white for the light areas.
children.note: The 1970s-80s shift from lead chromate and cadmium pigments toward these organic and titanium whites in packaging inks was driven by toxicity regulation, and is one of the reasons a 1982 box does not smell like a 1972 one.

children.name: Offset press (sheet-fed or web)
children.description: A printing press: plate cylinders, blanket cylinders, inking units, and either a sheet feed with a delivery stacker or a web unwind and rewind with a folder. For a corrugated box liner, the press is the capital equipment a converter owns.

facts.label: Units
facts.value: 2-6 inking units for up to 6 colours

children.name: Rainbow gradient (duotone / multi-stop blend)
children.description: Commodore's rainbow on the box and the case logo is a set of graded colour bands. On a flexo or litho box it is made either with a multi-colour duotone (the two separations overprinted at varying screen densities) or, on later short runs, printed with a spray/airbrush unit. This is where a printing shop makes one-off artwork effects cheaply.
children.note: The exact number of colours and whether the box used duotone or spray varies by printing run and region; the visual effect (a rainbow gradient band) is consistent across the packaging.

children.name: Varnish / water-based coating
children.description: A thin scuff-resistant coating over the printed board, applied on the press or in-line. It stops the rainbow rubbing off in the warehouse. Modern converters would use a water-based or UV-cure acrylic; 1982 used a solvent or water-based acryl.

children.name: Slotting, creasing, folding and gluing
children.description: The printed board goes through a slotter-creater which cuts the slots, scores the creases and trims the blanks; the blanks are then folded on a folder-gluer, which applies a hot starch or PVA glue to the tab and forms the box. It is a fast, near-fully-automated process.

facts.label: Adhesive
facts.value: PVA or hot-melt; starch for heavy board

facts.label: Throughput
facts.value: hundreds to thousands of boxes per hour

children.name: Parts tray for the loose items
children.description: Inside the box, below or beside the machine, the power cord, the A/V lead and the paperwork were either tied together in the foam or held in a separate moulded tray. Where a tray was used it was expanded polystyrene or, on later runs, a folded pulp tray.

facts.label: Materials used
facts.value: expanded polystyrene block, or moulded pulp

facts.label: Contents
facts.value: mains cord, A/V lead, manual, warranty card

children.note: I could not verify the exact internal arrangement of the C64 box by region and run. This node records that a tray or folded pulp cradle for the loose items existed as a class of 1980s arrangement, and flags the uncertainty rather than claiming a specific one.

children.name: Moulded polystyrene end blocks
children.description: Two white expanded-polystyrene blocks that cradle the ends of the machine so the case cannot be crushed in the box and cannot slide. They are moulded to the machine's outline in a steam-heated block mould, then cut down to size.

facts.label: Blowing agent
facts.value: chlorinated hydrocarbon (CFC-11 / dichloromethane), ~5-7% into the bead

children.note: EPS blocks were the standard protection for beige consumer electronics through the 1980s. Their disadvantage - they cannot be recycled with paper and they shatter into Styrofoam - is exactly why they vanished from Commodore's later packaging in favour of pulp and cardboard trays.

children.name: Expanded polystyrene (EPS)
children.description: Small beads of polystyrene, each already blown up with a chlorinated blowing agent, are heated and expanded again in a mould so the beads fuse into a solid block shaped to the part. The polymer is the same styrene copolymer chemistry as the ABS and the SAN; only the physical form is different.

children.name: EPS beads (expanded in a bead expander)
children.description: Styrene is suspension-polymerised in water to small beads, then a chlorinated blowing agent is dissolved into them under pressure; on heating the agent flashes and expands each bead from ~0.5-1 mm to 2-6 mm, and the beads are chilled and sieved by size.

facts.label: Blowing agent
facts.value: CFC-11 (trichlorofluoromethane) or dichloromethane, ~5-7 wt% in the bead

children.note: In 1982 the blowing agent was still a chlorinated hydrocarbon. Pentane is what you find in EPS today, but it only arrived after the 1987 Montreal Protocol drove CFC-11 out — so a period C64 is packed in ozone-depleting foam, which is why expanding or reprocessing thirty-year-old packaging is a regulated activity rather than a chore.

children.name: Chlorinated blowing agent (CFC-11 / dichloromethane)
children.description: Trichlorofluoromethane, or methylene chloride in the European trade. Both are excellent blowing agents: low boiling point, no flammability risk in the bead, and chemically inert enough to survive the polymerisation. They are also chlorinated, which is the whole problem — they destroy stratospheric ozone, so they were phased out of packaging foam through the 1990s and replaced by pentane and by butane.

facts.label: Why not then
facts.value: non-flammable, cheap, and already produced in bulk as a refrigerant

children.note: The fluorine came from fluorspar and the chlorine from the chlor-alkali cell — the same two mineral chains that make the etchant and the trichlorosilane elsewhere in this tree.

children.name: Bead expansion (bead expander)
children.description: Beads are fed into a steam-heated expander where they expand, are held at temperature to sinter them into a cake, and are then cooled and dried in a silo. The expander is the machine that sets the final foam density.

children.name: Block moulding in a steam-heated mould
children.description: Beads are blown into a heated aluminium mould and the steam expands them to fill it; the mould is then cooled and the block ejected. A block mould makes a slab that is later cut on a band saw or hot wire into the end blocks. The mould is a heat exchanger - the steam lines run through it.

facts.label: Cutting
facts.value: band saw or hot wire for complex profiles

children.note: Hot-wire cutting with a nichrome wire uses the same principle as a foam cup: a heated wire through a block. It is how the complex end-cap profiles were cut.

children.name: Polyethylene sleeve over the machine
children.description: A plain polyethylene bag over the boxed machine, to stop the moulded case and the printed manual from rubbing and to keep dust out during transit. It is a low-cost LDPE sleeve, blown as a tube on the same film-blowing line used for all commodity packaging film.

facts.label: Use
facts.value: dust and abrasion protection during distribution

children.note: Antistatic bags with an added conductive agent existed by the early 1980s but were not standard for a consumer computer at this price point; I could not verify an antistatic bag in the C64 box, so the bag is recorded as a plain polyethylene sleeve.

children.name: Film blowing and bag making
children.description: LDPE pellets are blown as a thin tube through a die and a bubble, cooled in an air ring, collapsed and wound; the tube is then cut and heat-sealed into a bag. Film blowing is high-volume and very cheap - the bag is cents, not dollars.

children.name: User's manual (fold-in-fold booklet)
children.description: The Commodore 64 user's manual - part 320974 in the service-manual parts list - is a cheap but well-made fold-in-fold booklet: a single sheet of coated wood-pulp paper printed in colour on both sides, folded twice with a 16-page section glued in the middle. It is the same construction as a road atlas, which is how a large amount of operating documentation was printed in 1982.

facts.label: Stock
facts.value: coated wood-pulp paper, ~60-100 gsm, colour both sides

facts.label: Binding
facts.value: 16-page fold-in-fold, glued on the centre spread

children.note: The C64 manual is well known for its fold-in-fold format and its colour printing on cheap stock - a deliberate cost decision on a product that was being sold through discount and supermarket channels. Some regional printings differ.

children.name: Coated printing paper
children.description: Wood-pulp paper filled and coated with clay (kaolin) and a binder, then calendered, so the ink sits on the surface and the colours are bright and sharp. It is the same stock as a supermarket leaflet.

facts.label: Fibre
facts.value: mostly softwood mechanical and kraft pulp

children.name: Colour offset printing of the manual
children.description: Sheet-fed offset litho in four colours (CMYK), plus spot colours for the Commodore rainbow and the red 'RESTORE' key highlights. The manual's diagrams and BASIC listings were set in hot-metal or phototypeset, then printed from plates.

facts.label: Prepress
facts.value: phototypesetting and photographic copy for the diagrams

children.note: Some C64 manuals have colour photography composited from transparencies, which is typical of pre-digital prepress in 1982: a mechanical or phototypeset page with a separately shot colour plate.

children.name: Fold-in-fold bindery
children.description: A long sheet is printed with the page imposition for a 16-page booklet, folded twice with a plate, and a 16-page section is glued into the middle crease. The result is a bound booklet that opens flat and costs almost nothing to assemble - it is pure paper engineering.

facts.label: Imposition
facts.value: 16 pages on one sheet, fold twice

facts.label: Adhesive
facts.value: PVA or hot-melt for the centre section

children.note: The fold-in-fold is the dominant cheap-booklet construction of the era and is why so many 1980s computer manuals fall open to the same two centre pages.

children.name: Letterpress covers (regional variants)
children.description: Some Commodore manuals and the box artwork of this period were printed letterpress from metal type on a platen or cylinder press rather than litho, and some C64 documentation was printed that way. Where a manual was letterpressed, the type impression is visible on the reverse and the cover has that slightly embossed, absorbent-paper look.

facts.label: Process
facts.value: relief printing from cast metal type or polymer plates

facts.label: Giveaway
facts.value: a slight debossed impression you can feel

children.note: Recorded because letterpress was still in use for 1980s Commodore collateral, but I could not verify that any particular C64 manual printing was letterpress rather than litho. Type metal would be lead-antimony, and the ink an oil-based printing ink of the same family as the box ink.

children.name: Warranty and registration card
children.description: A small printed card with the warranty terms and a serial-number registration slip. It is the same litho process as the manual on a heavier board stock, and it is the only part of the package with a legal function.
children.note: Warranty terms and the presence of a registration card varied by market; this node records the printed card as a class of object rather than claiming specific wording.

children.name: Shipping master carton and skid
children.description: Retail boxes were packed into corrugated master cartons, several to a carton, and banded on a timber skid for palletised shipping from the Hong Kong or Taiwan assembly plant to a regional warehouse. Skids - not euro-pallets - were the norm for export shipping of this period.

facts.label: Master carton
facts.value: double-wall corrugated, usually printed stencilled with contents and count

facts.label: Skid
facts.value: sawn timber skid with a bearers, no deckboards

facts.label: Strapping
facts.value: steel or polypropylene band around the carton

children.name: Timber skid
children.description: A wooden skid: three or more bearers with a top deck, or a bare skid with the cartons loaded straight onto it. Skids are made from rough-sawn softwood offcuts, which is why they are the cheapest way to make a heavy load forkable.

children.name: Rough-sawn softwood
children.description: Kiln-dried or green softwood, band-sawn to bearers and deckboards. The sawmill waste that cannot be pulped into paper - knots, ends, slabs - is exactly what a skid is made of, which is a neat closure of the wood chain.

facts.label: Moisture
facts.value: green or kiln-dried, depending on the shipping leg

children.name: Strapping (steel or polypropylene)
children.description: Steel band with a stamped seal, or the polypropylene strapping that had largely displaced it by the 1980s because it does not rust, does not cut the carton and is lighter to ship back as waste.

children.name: Master-carton board
children.description: Heavier double-wall corrugated, usually a recycled medium and recycled liners, with the shipping marks stencilled or flexo-printed rather than litho-printed.

children.name: Final pack-out and pack-out line
children.description: At the end of the case-moulding and assembly plant, machines are bagged, placed in the foam blocks, dropped into the printed box with the manual and card, and the box is closed and labelled. This was semi-automatic and was the labour-heavy step that determined where a home computer was finally assembled.

facts.label: Operations
facts.value: bag, foam, box, insert paper, close, label, case-pack

facts.label: Labour
facts.value: a few operators per line; the constraint on Commodore's throughput

children.note: Pack-out in Hong Kong and Taiwan in the early 1980s was where the cost advantage of shipping a nearly-finished machine - rather than a finished one - to be finished and packed in Asia was actually realised.

roots.name: Decoration: legends, logos and metallised inks on plastic
roots.description: Getting colour and type onto moulded plastic in 1982 meant printing it, not moulding colour into it. Commodore used two-colour pad printing for the keycap legends and the rainbow badge, screen printing where a flat surface allowed it, metallised flake ink for the shiny logo bars, and - in later production - two-shot moulding and painted or lacquered surfaces. Each process has its own pad, ink, screen and cure chemistry.
roots.note: The dominant decorating process on a 1982 C64 is pad printing, because the parts are curved, crowned, textured and one-shot moulded - none of which suit screen printing. Two-shot moulding and in-mould labelling existed but were expensive and not used on the breadbin case.

children.name: Pad printing (tampo printing)
children.description: The workhorse process. A soft silicone rubber pad is pressed onto a flat metal cliche carrying the image in wet ink, picks the ink up on its raised relief, then deforms against the curved or crowned plastic part and transfers the image. One pad, one colour, one station; two stations give the two-colour keycap legends.

facts.label: Throughput
facts.value: hundreds to thousands of impressions per hour

facts.label: Surface tolerance
facts.value: curved, crowned and textured parts, unlike screen printing

children.name: Two-colour pad printing press
children.description: A small cast frame with a plate table, an ink cup or doctor blade, a silicone pad on a shuttle head, and part fixtures on a rotating or indexing table. Each colour station is one table position with its own pad.

facts.label: Registration
facts.value: micro-adjustable pad alignment; the hard part on a keycap

children.note: Registration on a two-colour legend is the skill of the job: the second impression has to land exactly on top of the first, shifted symbols and all.

children.name: Silicone rubber printing pad
children.description: A soft, solvent-resistant, low-surface-energy pad - almost always silicone rubber - cut or cast with the relief to pick up and transfer the image. It is the consumable that has to be replaced every few thousand impressions, and pad choice (hardness, hardness-to-image ratio) is the operator's main variable.

facts.label: Life
facts.value: thousands to tens of thousands of impressions

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: two-part cast pad with a hardened steel or aluminium backing

children.name: Two-part silicone pad compound
children.description: A polydimethylsiloxane casting system cured at room temperature with a tin catalyst or an addition-cure platinum system. Pads are cast in a mould against the plate image so the relief matches exactly.

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: room temperature, ~24 h; or heat-accelerated addition cure

children.note: The same PDMS chemistry as the switch contact pad; a 1982 pad-printing shop and a keyboard switch factory were buying essentially the same silicone.

children.name: Cliche (the printing plate) and its electrotype
children.description: The image is held in a flat copper or nickel electrotype, or a photopolymer plate, sunk into a plate table and flooded with ink. The traditional route is a photograph on a copper plate, which is electroplated up to 0.5-1 mm and then hand- or machine-polished back to leave only the image proud - the electrotype.
children.note: A flat pad-print cliche is a simpler object than a litho plate because there is no water damping - it is essentially a stencil on a copper block, which is why pad printing was chosen for short runs as well as long ones.

children.name: Photopolymer plate
children.description: A photosensitive polymer film laminated to a steel backing, exposed through a film negative, washed out to leave the image in relief, and cured. It replaced the electrotype for short runs because it needs no electroplating step.

facts.label: Negative
facts.value: film or glass, from the artwork

children.note: This is the prepress step the whole packaging and decoration industry shared with offset lithography in 1982: artwork went to a camera or a phototypesetter, and plates were contact-printed from film.

children.name: Copper electrotyping of the plate
children.description: The sensitised copper plate is electroplated in an acid copper bath to build a thick deposit on the image, then the surface is ground and polished back so only the image stands proud. It is an old, slow process, but it gives an image hard enough to print millions of impressions.

facts.label: Bath
facts.value: acidified copper sulphate with an additive

children.name: Pad-printing ink (solvent or UV)
children.description: A free-flowing, low-viscosity ink that will transfer off a soft pad and then dry on a plastic part. In 1982 most pad inks were solvent-based (glycol ether / xylene / ester solvent with an alkyd or acrylic resin and a pigment); UV-curing pad inks existed and were gaining ground, and were faster but needed a lamp.

children.name: Ink binder resin (alkyd or acrylic)
children.description: The film-forming part of the ink: an alkyd built from drying-oil fatty acids and a polyacid (the same chemistry as the printing ink vehicle on the box), or an acrylic copolymer. It is chosen for adhesion to ABS, which is notoriously hard to print on without a surface treatment.
children.note: ABS has a low surface energy and low surface tension (~38-39 dynes/cm, against ~72 for water), which is why printing ink on it needs a good wetting binder or a plasma/corona treatment - and why the legends on a forty-year-old cap can be abraded off but not easily peeled.

children.name: Legend and logo pigments
children.description: The legend white is almost always titanium dioxide in an alkyd binder; the rainbow logo uses a set of saturated organic pigments - phthalocyanine blue, quinacridone magenta, azo yellow - and sometimes a metallised flake for the bright bars.
children.note: The same pigment supply chain as the case masterbatch and the box ink: a set of convergences that all end at the same handful of chemical plants.

children.name: Ink solvent (glycol ether / ester blend)
children.description: The volatile carrier that gives pad ink its low viscosity. Common 1980s pad-ink solvents were propylene glycol ethers, dibutyl phthalate or xylene blends. It flashes off the pad quickly enough to give a sharp print and slowly enough that the impression can be placed.
children.note: Solvent-based pad ink is largely gone from consumer goods today because of VOC regulation; UV-curing pad ink, which needs no solvent at all, is the modern replacement and was already available in 1982.

children.name: Propylene oxide (for the glycol ether solvent)
children.description: Made by the chlorohydrin route (propylene + chlorine + water, then caustic dehydrochlorination) or the older hydroperoxide route (propylene + hydroperoxide, then a base-catalysed rearrangement). It is what turns propylene into propylene glycol ethers and acetates, the commonest 1980s pad-ink and screen-ink solvent.

facts.label: Chlorohydrin route
facts.value: additive chlorination then dehydrochlorination with Ca(OH)2

facts.label: Glycol ether
facts.value: propylene oxide + alcohol (e.g. n-propyl) at base, then distillation

children.note: A pad-printing ink is therefore not a purely cosmetic chemical: its main solvent begins at the same propylene that feeds the acrylonitrile in the ABS case.

children.name: UV curing of ink
children.description: A mercury or metal-halide lamp floods the printed part in under a second and the photo-initiator in the ink polymerises it in place. It was the big printing-technology change of the late 1970s and early 1980s: instant cure, no solvent, no oven, and a harder, more abrasion-resistant print.
children.note: By 1982 UV curing was established in screen printing and pad printing on plastics but not yet universal; solvent drying was still the volume route. Its big advantage for a decoration shop is that you can print a keycap and immediately stack it with no drying time.

children.name: Screen printing
children.description: Silk screening through a mesh, used on Commodore parts where the surface is flat enough: printed panels, keycap sets on flat-topped caps, cartridge labels and some case markings. It cannot print the grain-textured bezel reliably, which is exactly why pad printing won on the case.

facts.label: Mesh
facts.value: nylon monofilament or stainless steel wire, 100-200 mesh

facts.label: Ink
facts.value: one-part epoxy or solvent ink, cured by UV or heat

children.name: Screen mesh (nylon monofilament or stainless wire)
children.description: A woven mesh stretched and glued to an aluminium frame. Nylon is used where solvent or epoxy inks would attack a wire screen; stainless wire is used where long life under abrasive inks matters. Both are woven from a drawn filament or wire on a loom.

facts.label: Count
facts.value: ~100-200 mesh for fine legends, coarser for solid areas

children.note: The nylon is hexamethylenediamine + adipic acid again - the same PA6,6 that goes into connector latches, drawn down to 50-80 um for the mesh.

children.name: Screen emulsion (PVA or diazo)
children.description: The photosensitive coating that becomes the stencil. Diazo emulsions, standard in 1982, are washed out with water after exposure; PVA emulsion requires a separate exposure through the base and is more solvent-resistant. The stencil is exposed through a film positive and then washed.

children.name: Squeegee blade
children.description: A rubber or neoprene blade in a wooden or aluminium holder that forces ink through the stencil and wipes the surface. The durometer of the blade is the operator's variable: hard for fine detail, soft for heavy coverage.

children.name: Neoprene squeegee rubber
children.description: Polychloroprene, chosen because it resists the solvents in screen ink and wears well. It is the same chloroprene rubber used for cable jackets and gaskets, again pointing back to the C4 cracker cut.

children.name: Screen-printing ink (one-part epoxy)
children.description: A one-component epoxy or polyester ink with a latent hardener, screen-printed through the stencil and then heat-cured. Epoxy ink is unusually durable on plastics and is what screen-printed Commodore product panels and keycap overlays used.
children.note: One-part epoxy inks cure at 120-150 C for 5-20 minutes, or flash to UV if the formulation is UV-curable. The epoxy supply chain (bisphenol A + epichlorohydrin) is documented under c64.case.other-polymers.epoxy.

children.name: Metallised and pearlescent ink
children.description: The shiny bars in the Commodore rainbow logo and the metallic trim on some panels are metallised ink: pigment-grade aluminium flake, or vacuum-metallised polyester film, suspended in a binder and printed, then optionally burnished to align the flakes flat so they reflect.

facts.label: Flake
facts.value: atomised aluminium, ~5-15 um, or vacuum-metallised polyester film

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: a flat mirror-like metallic that changes with viewing angle

children.note: Flake ink is genuinely a compromise: randomly oriented flakes only reflect a fraction of the light, so metallised ink looks duller than metal - unless it is burnished, which is why a good logo feels smoother than the plastic around it.

children.name: Atomised aluminium flake
children.description: Molten aluminium is atomised with air into 5-15 um flakes, which are then washed, sifted by size and coated with an oxidation-inhibiting lacquer so they do not go grey. The same basic process makes the aluminium in the EMI shield, only at a different scale.

facts.label: Passivation
facts.value: lacquer or chromate wash to stop further oxidation

children.note: Aluminium flake pigment for inks is a genuinely old chemistry - used in water-based paints and print metallic inks since the nineteenth century.

children.name: Binder for metallised ink (acrylic or alkyd)
children.description: A drying ink binder that holds the flakes flat and lets them reflect. Formulated so the flake lies parallel to the surface; this is what produces the flat metallic look rather than a sparkly one.

children.name: Burnishing (or calendering) the flake
children.description: Passing the printed part between heated polished rollers flattens the flakes into the surface so they mirror rather than scatter. Burnished metallic ink on a moulded part looks like a metal panel - which is precisely the intent of a rainbow badge.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: heated roller calender between nylon or paper rolls

children.name: Hot foil stamping (alternative to flake ink)
children.description: A heated metal foil is pressed onto the plastic with a type plate and the image transfers. On rigid ABS this needs a rougher surface or a soft stamping die, which is why flake ink beat foil stamping on a textured case - but foil stamping was used on smooth panels and on some packaging.
children.note: Included because it is the era's standard metallic-decoration alternative and because the 'mirror' finish on some Commodore trim is hot-stamped film rather than ink.

children.name: Two-shot / in-mould decoration
children.description: Deciding not to print at all and moulding the colour or the decoration in: a second shot in a second colour, or an in-mould printed film or transfer placed in the tool before the shot. Both existed in 1982 but were expensive, and neither is used on the breadbin case - the colour there is pigment in the resin.

facts.label: In-mould printing
facts.value: a pre-printed film or decal placed in the tool, flooded with resin

facts.label: In-mould labelling
facts.value: a printed label applied to the core of the tool before moulding

children.note: In-mould decoration is scratch-proof and cycle-fast, which is why it became the norm for later consumer plastics; for a 1982 breadbin case the cost was not justified. The idea that the legend is part of the plastic rather than on it did not become common until the 1990s.

children.name: Spray lacquer and paint (used on accessories, not the case)
children.description: Spray-applied lacquer over plastic - used on joystick housings, on some panels and on plastic accessory parts - was an acrylic or nitrocellulose lacquer, sprayed in a ventilated booth and stoved at 60-80 C. It is how a plastic part gets a uniform, slightly textured finish that hides mould flow marks.
children.note: I could not confirm that the C64 case itself was sprayed, and the beige ABS is normally unpainted; spray lacquering is included because it was routine on the plastic accessories and on some case variants, and because the haze it gives is what is sometimes mistaken for 'moulded-in colour'.

children.name: Spray lacquer (acrylic or nitrocellulose)
children.description: A solvent-borne film former with pigment, sprayed and baked. Nitrocellulose was standard for consumer plastic coatings in 1982; 2K polyurethane and water-borne acrylic were the better performers but more expensive and better suited to metal.

children.name: Cure oven (batch, gas-fired)
children.description: A batch oven with gas burners and forced circulation, holding 60-80 C for 20-30 minutes to flash off the solvent and crosslink the lacquer. The gas burners are the only fossil fuel on the decorating line.

children.name: Keycap legend overlays and printed inserts
children.description: An alternative to printing the cap is to bond a printed film or a moulded insert onto or into the cap. Commodore keycaps are printed, not overlaid, but the technique was in use on contemporary keyboards and appears on some Commodore accessories and on the memory-expansion modules. Recorded here for completeness with low confidence for the C64 specifically.

facts.label: Technique
facts.value: screen-printed polyester film bonded into a recess, or a two-shot printed insert

children.note: Unverified for the 1982 breadbin C64 keycaps. What is verified is that the caps are moulded ABS with printed legends, with the font weight, legend position and printed faces varying between production runs - which is itself a good way to date a keyboard.

children.name: Decoration inspection (100% look)
children.description: Printed parts are checked for legibility, registration and offset before they go into the machine. On a two-colour legend, a shift by half a character width is a reject, so this is a genuinely tight tolerance - and one of the reasons legends look so consistent on surviving machines.

facts.label: Tolerance
facts.value: registration to a fraction of a character width

children.name: Prepress: artwork to printing film and plate
children.description: Every legend and every logo started as artwork, which in 1982 was mechanically or photographically composed, then copied onto film by a process camera, and the film was used to expose a plate. Text was set in hot metal or phototype, and the Commodore rainbow artwork was assembled from painted separations by hand.

facts.label: Text setting
facts.value: hot metal or phototypesetting (later CRT phototype)

children.note: The C64 rainbow is one of the most reproduced pieces of 1980s graphic design, and it was made the slow way: separations drawn and painted, then screened. There was no desktop publishing until the late 1980s.

children.name: Ortho photographic film (negative)
children.description: The black-and-white film that carries the image to the plate. It is a cellulose or polyester film coated with a silver-halide emulsion; exposed in a process camera or a contact frame, then developed and fixed in a chemical line.

children.name: Film base (cellulose triacetate or polyester)
children.description: A flexible transparent film on which the emulsion is cast. Cellulose triacetate was the standard photographic film base, made from acetic anhydride and cellulose; polyester (PET) film base became common later for its dimensional stability.
children.note: The cellulose comes from wood pulp (a dissolved pulp paper route) and the acetic acid from methanol oxidation - so a printing negative is partly wood and partly natural gas.

children.name: Acetic acid / acetic anhydride for film base
children.description: Made by catalytic oxidation of ethanol, or by the carbonylation of methanol. Methanol comes from synthesis gas, which comes from natural-gas reforming.

facts.label: Carbonylation
facts.value: methanol + CO -> acetic acid, rhodium catalyst, 150-200 C

children.name: Cellulose (for triacetate)
children.description: Dissolved from wood pulp and regenerated into fibre. The film route is a small, high-purity use of cellulose compared with paper, but it is the same feedstock: a tree.

children.name: Silver halide emulsion
children.description: Silver bromide or silver iodide crystals suspended in gelatin. The silver comes from silver ore, and most photographic silver of the era was recovered as a byproduct of lead and copper refining rather than mined for itself.

children.name: Silver (recovered from ore and refinery residue)
children.description: Silver metal recovered from argentite and galena ores, and from the anode slimes of electrolytic copper refining. It is refined to photographic purity by cupellation and electrolytic refining.

facts.label: Recovery
facts.value: mostly a byproduct of lead/copper refining

children.name: Galena (lead sulfide ore) and silver-bearing concentrates
children.description: Galena is the dominant lead ore and almost always carries silver as argentite or as silver dissolved in the galena lattice. It is mined, concentrated by flotation, and reduced in a blast furnace or sinter plant.

children.name: Cupellation of lead bullion
children.description: Lead bullion is oxidised in a cupellation furnace; the litharge formed is absorbed back into the bath and the noble metal - silver and gold - floats as dross on top. The silver is then refined electrolytically to photographic purity.
children.note: So the legend on a keycap is, several steps down, partly silver that came out of a lead ore in a cupellation furnace.

children.name: Electrolytic refining of silver
children.description: Crude silver from the cupellation hearth is dissolved in nitric acid and electrolytically refined: silver anodes, silver-nitrate electrolyte, pure silver cathodes. The result is 99.99% silver - the purity photographic chemistry needs for its emulsion.

facts.label: Electrolyte
facts.value: silver nitrate in aqueous nitric acid

children.name: Silver nitrate
children.description: Made by dissolving silver in hot nitric acid. Silver nitrate is the classic photographic salt: reacting it with halide in gelatin is what makes the silver-halide grains in a film or paper negative.

children.name: Nitric acid (Ostwald process)
children.description: Ammonia is oxidised to nitric oxide over a platinum-rhodium gauze at 800-950 C, to nitrogen dioxide, and absorbed in water to give nitric acid. The ammonia comes from natural gas via steam reforming and Haber-Bosch synthesis.

facts.label: Absorption
facts.value: NO2 absorbed in water in a packed column

children.note: The same nitric acid that dissolves the silver also oxidises cyclohexanol to adipic acid for the nylon latches in the connectors. One chemical, several very different products.
